# 15. Architecture and tools

This chapter is about the program underneath a roguelike and the tools around it. It covers how to structure code so that hundreds of interacting kinds of content stay manageable, how to keep the rules apart from what the player sees, and how to build the editors, validators, debug views and servers that let a small team iterate on a generated game and see inside it. It matters because a roguelike's content keeps growing and keeps wanting exceptions, and an architecture that cannot absorb them slows everything else down: Danny Day watched Desktop Dungeons' release cadence slip from weekly to every two months for exactly that reason ([Danny Day 2018, 3:55](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=235)).

The talks come at the subject mostly from shipped games and the people who built them, with toolmakers and a few researchers alongside. What makes them useful together is how often they converge. Developers working on very different games arrive at content held in data, behaviour split into small decoupled units, and a deterministic simulation sealed off from its presentation. Brian Cronin lists what solid architecture of this kind makes achievable: determinism, saves, replays, networking, undo, previews and testing ([Brian Cronin 2024, 3:03](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=183)). The chapter follows that path from the diagnosis to the architecture to its payoffs, then turns to tools, validation, visibility, foundations and performance.

## In brief

- A roguelike's architectural problem is breadth, not depth: very many kinds of content, each tempted to become a special case, so plan around special cases rather than hoping clean data structures will make them go away ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 10:18](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=618); [Kate Compton 2016, 13:03](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=783); [Kate Compton 2016, 24:56](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1496)).
- Write the rules once in a well-tested engine and author content as data that it interprets, as Tracery, Ultimate ADOM, Caves of Qud, Cataclysm, Hades and Backpack Hero all do, while keeping an escape hatch into code for effects the data format cannot yet express ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:43](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=823); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:58](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=958); [Ray 2023, 2:39](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=159); [Jeremy Rose 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=545); [Alice Lai 2021, 15:39](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=939); [Jasper Cole 2023, 7:57](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=477); [Brian Cronin 2021, 12:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=725)).
- Pull behaviour out of entities into small, separately addressable units (actions, commands or event handlers) so that each new behaviour does not need to know about every other one ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 17:18](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1038); [Bob Nystrom 2018, 18:53](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1133); [Danny Day 2018, 5:33](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=333); [Brian Cronin 2024, 16:36](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=996); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 29:05](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1745)).
- Isolate the simulation from its presentation: one serialisable state including the random number generator, control that flows one way, and a presentation layer that learns about the world only from emitted change records ([Brian Cronin 2024, 8:54](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=534); [Brian Cronin 2024, 13:31](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=811); [Brian Cronin 2024, 20:11](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1211); [Brian Cronin 2021, 21:51](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1311); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=564)).
- A deterministic simulation whose initial state and stream of commands or events can be recorded gives you saves, replays, bug reproduction, server-side verification and lockstep networking, but determinism has to be designed in from the start ([Brian Cronin 2024, 25:33](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1533); [Danny Day 2018, 18:52](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1132); [Colin Liotta 2018, 7:08](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=428); [Brian Cronin 2021, 8:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=486); [Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:42](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1302)).
- Pick the cheapest networking model your game's tolerance for input lag allows: turn-based games usually manage with deterministic lockstep, and rollback is for games, like a rhythm game, that cannot wait a round trip ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 3:03](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=183); [Tyriq Plummer 2025, 8:47](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=527); [Tyriq Plummer 2025, 9:10](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=550); [Scott Anderson 2026, 4:38:44](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16724)).
- If you want modding, plan for it from the start, build your own content with the same system, and require mods to declare an API version from day one ([George Moromisato 2022, 18:48](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1128); [Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:08](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=308); [Dylan Gedig 2022, 28:19](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1699); [George Moromisato 2022, 19:45](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1185); [George Moromisato 2022, 25:49](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1549)).
- Judge a tool by its turnaround, the time between making a change and seeing it in the running game, and cut the cost of the operations you do several times a minute ([JP LeBreton 2019, 11:34](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=694); [Leigh Alexander 2023, 29:49](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1789); [JP LeBreton 2019, 8:55](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=535); [Colin Liotta 2018, 8:44](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=524); [Chris McCormick 2021, 24:15](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1455)).
- Check data automatically where independently authored pieces meet, and let a machine play the real game headlessly to catch crashes and unwinnable builds before human testers see them ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 5:29](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=329); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 20:19](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1219); [Jeremy Rose 2022, 16:49](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1009); [Phenry Ewing 2022, 26:56](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1616); [Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 21:32](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1292); [Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 22:27](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1347)).
- A procedural game has no static scene to inspect, so build visibility in: an extensible debug menu early, raw data recorded from every run, and crash reports that arrive with the save and the trace attached ([Alexander Birke 2024, 8:38](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=518); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 18:46](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1126); [Alan Malloy 2017, 12:55](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=775); [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:44](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=224); [Alan Malloy 2017, 23:07](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1387); [Drew Streib 2016, 16:02](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=962)).

## Why roguelike code rots: breadth, special cases and coupling

### The problem is breadth, not depth

Most game architecture advice was written for games whose hard problems sit inside each entity: physics, animation, rendering. Bob Nystrom argues that a roguelike's problem is different. Its entities do many different things, from inventory management to special effects, and there are a great many of them: he sets Fortnite's roughly sixteen kinds of monster against the 317 or so that Angband's wiki lists. That breadth, he says, is an organisational challenge rather than a technical one ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 10:18](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=618)).

Breadth would be manageable if each piece of content behaved like the others. It does not. Kate Compton points out that roguelikes need lots of content and each piece tends to want custom behaviour, such as a different sound for the axe and the hammer ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:03](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=783)). And the problem gets worse as the game gets better: chess has few special cases, but a world full of weird generated things that should do something funny on the 4th of July is special cases forever. The more interesting the world, the more common and the more interesting its special cases become, so you should plan around them rather than hope clean data structures will make them go away ([Kate Compton 2016, 24:56](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1496)).

### How it goes wrong

The talks describe the same failure from several directions, and the convergence is worth taking seriously.

- **The if-chain.** Compton's warning sign is a giant chain of if statements in content logic. Its cost is repeated once per piece of content, or worse, so that is the moment to stop and design a data structure ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:03](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=783)).
- **The interaction matrix.** George Moromisato shows the same thing as a table: three swords times three creatures is nine cases to program, with a flaming sword doing extra damage to a yeti but something else to a dragon. Under modding the matrix becomes unfillable, because if one mod adds a fireball and another adds a magic creature, nobody decides what the one does to the other ([George Moromisato 2022, 5:26](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=326)).
- **Special cases spread through an inheritance hierarchy.** Day describes Desktop Dungeons' inheritance-based prototype, where gods spread through the code "like fungus". A god that disliked throwing needed a worship check on every throw; one that liked flying needed checks whenever an entity's movement changed. Every prototyping change meant rebuilding these tendrils, and the release cadence slipped from weekly to every two months ([Danny Day 2018, 3:55](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=235)).
- **Managers that call each other.** Brian Cronin's example is an upgrade that says "when taking damage, discard the top card": the card manager calls the damage manager, which calls the upgrade manager, which calls back into the card manager mid-play. The code can re-enter itself and nothing owns anything, which makes replays and networking hard. He is strict about avoiding global state and singletons ([Brian Cronin 2024, 8:01](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=481)).
- **Logic mixed with presentation.** On Monster Train, cards called managers that called back into objects, with on-discard effects triggered after animations, until everything relied on global access and, by late development, Cronin felt the codebase was a set of wires not to touch. He adds that Unity's game objects invite this by encouraging you to put lights, models and logic in one place ([Brian Cronin 2021, 20:44](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1244)).

Old code rots in a further way: it accumulates assumptions about platforms and presentation. Thomas Biskup explains that modernising ADOM with graphics, sound and a modern UI was slow because the team was not building a new game but working on ancient legacy code never planned for anything graphical ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 21:25](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1285)). NetHack's developers found that porting code for many systems combined with compile-time optional features made the source hard to navigate, so they made many options permanent to simplify it ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 19:32](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=1172)). Flexibility you do not use is still code you have to read.

### The counter-moves

Against this, the talks offer a small set of moves that recur in very different games.

**Decouple behaviours so complexity grows linearly.** Nystrom's actions (covered below) are fairly independent of each other, which lets him keep adding behaviours without feeling the quadratic complexity of the codebase getting worse ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 18:53](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1133)). The point is not the action class itself but that each new behaviour should not have to know about every other one.

**Turn verbs into nouns.** Nystrom generalises this into a technique he says has always worked for him: when code lacks flexibility, take a verb in the program and make it an object. The operation can then be created in one place, run in another and given extra properties. The command pattern also makes undo in a level editor straightforward, because each command can undo itself and history is just a list of commands ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 20:40](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1240)).

**Design each system in isolation with plug points.** Joel Clark describes how Blaseball adds mechanics on the fly: each system is designed as its own thing with a clean purpose and defined points other systems can call. A team roster is just a list of players with ways to add or remove one; other systems plug in to add a player, incinerate one or swap one with another team ([Joel Clark 2020, 26:22](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1582)). On top of that, a modification players can carry can link any two systems together or add new rules to an existing system ([Joel Clark 2020, 27:29](https://youtu.be/zO05p-e57AQ?t=1649)). Scott Kovach makes a related point about rule-based logic: behaviour can often be changed by appending rules or adding higher-priority ones, rather than editing old code ([Scott Kovach 2019, 29:43](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=1783)).

**Reuse a system when the new thing fits its definition.** Kristen Yu describes a game at Improbable that had content explicitly called quests and other content that looked like quests but was not labelled as such. Recognising that these quest-like objects fit the general definition of a quest let the team deliver them through the existing quest system instead of building a second one ([Kristen Yu 2021, 9:18](https://youtu.be/WutTZ4FCHA8?t=558)).

**Leave uniform hooks.** Alexei Pepers points to NetHack's per-slot equip functions: equipping boots of levitation runs the boots function, and there is a function for shields even though, as the comment notes, no shield needs special handling yet. The format stays uniform and future features or mods have somewhere to go; Pepers calls writing code a little further than strictly needed a brilliant way to save future problems ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 18:19](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1099)).

### Abstraction is not free

Structure has its own failure mode. Compton, whose advice runs through this chapter, admits that her specification-driven parser for any Tracery-like language, meant to generate programs and build editors automatically, was way overly complicated and probably not that useful; she changed direction after it ([Kate Compton 2020, 25:57](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1557)). And a structure can quietly stop doing the job it was built for. In Stav Hinenzon's Sunshine Shuffle the chore queue was meant to show what was coming up, but responsibility drifted to the graph parser, chores rarely sat in the queue more than a few frames, and the queue ended up as little more than a tie-breaker for things that had to lock everything else ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 11:08](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=668)).

The practical rule that emerges is Compton's: introduce structure when you see the same kind of special case being written over and over, not before ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:03](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=783)). When you do, design for the special cases you know are coming rather than for every case you can imagine.

### Why it pays

Cronin gives the strongest reason to invest. Solid gameplay architecture is what makes determinism, save and load, networking, replays, undo and redo, effect previews and testing achievable. On Inkbound players could send replay files, often automatically, to reproduce bugs; on Monster Train the card-outcome preview was hard to implement precisely because the architecture was not solid ([Brian Cronin 2024, 3:03](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=183)). The rest of this chapter is largely about how to get those benefits.

## Content as data: rules in the engine, things in files

### Don't whittle your own screws

If one position in this chapter has near-universal support, it is this: write the rules once, in an engine, and write the content as data that the engine interprets. Compton frames it as "don't whittle your own screws". Indie developers keep hand-making one-off solutions for each new connection problem, but most content needs fairly standard behaviour, so you should make a standard data structure for it, or better, find one (often in academic work), author many pieces as static data and run them all through one interpreter. Because there is only one interpreter, you can build and test it well; she credits this for Tracery's stability ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:43](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=823)). Her example of the payoff is Twine: once hypertext was formalised as nodes, text and links with an interpreter, many non-programmers built immense structures without writing a single if statement ([Kate Compton 2016, 15:05](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=905)).

> A lot of content requires pretty standard behavior, so make a standard data structure for it, or better yet find one. — [Kate Compton 2016, 13:43](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=823)

Biskup describes the same shape at the scale of a whole game. Ultimate ADOM is a core rules engine that knows all rules, interactions and subsystems, driven by an external configuration that describes items, monsters, quests and the rest, with platform-specific UIs and platform configurations (mobile versus desktop, for example) layered on top ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 15:58](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=958)). The motivation is the one Compton gives: you should not have to hide the rules of your game deep in code behind if-then-else special cases, and externalised data makes modding much easier ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 3:50](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=230)).

### The same move, game after game

The pattern shows up in very different projects, which is the best evidence that it is right:

- **Caves of Qud** defines content in XML files arranged in an inheritance tree; objects inherit properties from parents and can mix in others, and modders can overlay a partial definition that rewrites precise parts of the data tree ([Ray 2023, 2:39](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=159)). Ray lists how much sits in data: items, creatures, conversations, quests, population tables (what the game uses to pick random items), factions, books, player presets, even custom genders and pronouns ([Ray 2023, 3:25](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=205)).
- **Cataclysm** defines all its nouns (items, monsters, terrain, furniture, which limbs a character has, martial arts) and many of its verbs in JSON, according to Jeremy Rose ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=545)).
- **Ultimate ADOM** uses JSON templates with inheritance, parameterised components and slots. A wall inherits from tile, which inherits from thing; it has a relative-size component, a parameterless "solid" component that blocks movement, and a material slot set to stone carrying resistances and hit point formulas. An orc warrior is a being with default equipment, profession and race slots and a default goal of killing the player that level definitions can override. Biskup chose JSON because modding then needs only a text editor ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 16:45](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1005)).
- **Hades** implements boons and hammers as traits. Alice Lai explains that every ability is defined by numbers in JSON (the Ares Blade Rift projectile has piercing, speed, range, damage rate, impact velocity, where zero means no knockback, and duration), and a trait adds, subtracts, multiplies or toggles those attributes ([Alice Lai 2021, 15:39](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=939)).
- **Backpack Hero** started with hand-coded items, which forced items to be simple. Jasper Cole describes the refactor to an "item2" system in which an item is configured in the Unity inspector from drop-downs of trigger, effect, value and target: the wooden sword is "on use, damage, 7, selected enemy". Most of the roughly 865 items use it, and modders can use the same system ([Jasper Cole 2023, 7:57](https://youtu.be/COeJTtSDd78?t=477)).
- **Monster Train** represents a card as data pointing to parameterised effect scripts. Torch has a CardEffectDamage effect with a target mode and an integer; its description text hooks into that value, so changing the damage from 2 to 3 updates the card text in every language without re-translation ([Brian Cronin 2021, 10:09](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=609)).
- **Spry Fox** keeps most design content in YAML. Patrick Kemp's reason is that text files are searchable, support find-and-replace and copy-paste, and let designers use mature IDEs and their extensions instead of custom editors; graphical tools are kept for things like terrain and set pieces ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 3:34](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=214)). Configs can include named, reusable blocks, both for boilerplate and to compose behaviour from several sources, and are expanded at generation time into the final configs the engine reads ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 6:58](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=418)).
- **Angband and Sil-Q** keep monster and item attributes, placement, names and tile assignments in text files. That let Joel Ryan, a non-programmer, do all of Sil-Q's tile assignment himself, cutting an inherited 4,600-line file down to about 1,400 lines ([Joel Ryan 2022, 8:41](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=521)).

The same move works for behaviour that looks like it must be code. Johnathan Pagnutti expresses a Slay the Spire enemy's state machine as two tables: a states table giving each move's block, damage and strength, and a transitions table of probabilities, so a row reads "60% of the time after Chomp, Jaw Worm will Bellow" ([Johnathan Pagnutti 2025, 5:39](https://youtu.be/Uf34SbuWIos?t=339)). Paris Buttfield-Addison describes Yarn Spinner node groups that act either as pools, where many nodes qualify and the least-seen one is dealt out (rooms, random events, barks), or as rules, where conditions do not overlap so exactly one passes: an if-else in which each branch can be added without touching the others ([Paris Buttfield-Addison 2026, 6:35:56](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=23756)). The shape of the data matters too. Liza Knipscher moved Bioloom's creature genes from a recursive tree, which was impossible to work with, to a flat list of body parts, each with a path of socket IDs (an eye at 0, 0, 1 is on torso socket zero, then the second position on the head), with colour and size layered on top ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 32:40](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1960)).

### What data buys you

The talks name a consistent set of benefits:

- **Safety and reuse.** Compton notes that JSON content can be copied in large chunks from someone else's work, checked with an online linter, and run safely even when strangers wrote it. George Buckenham's server runs around 500 strangers' bots without restarts, which she says would be inadvisable with arbitrary JavaScript ([Kate Compton 2016, 11:02](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=662)).
- **Authors who are not programmers.** Benjamin Berman observes that when you get other people to write cards, the first thing they feel is that they do not want to write code; he points to Paradox games and Civilization as succeeding with modding through big structured data ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 22:35](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1355)). Ryan's tile work on Sil-Q is the same point in practice ([Joel Ryan 2022, 8:41](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=521)).
- **Tools that see the whole game.** Because Cataclysm is data, Rose could build an external guide that indexes it, after answering questions by hand-searching for an item's ID and then for what dropped it became too tedious ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 9:05](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=545)). Data has structure you must respect, though: showing where an item spawns meant collapsing palette, mapgen and location into one apparent link, and he would consider a triple store for richer queries if rebuilding ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 27:08](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1628)).
- **Future generators.** Berman adds that structured card data suits future card generators; in his view the obstacle to machine-learned card generation is a large dataset of cards in a usable representation ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 22:35](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1355)).

### Where data stops

Data-driven design has limits, and the talks are specific about where they are.

The first is expressiveness. Cronin found Monster Train's script-per-effect cards worked for independent, linear effects but broke down when effects depended on each other or scaled. X-cost cards like Vent relied on invisible card traits that modified damage implicitly inside a character's bonus-damage calculation, so designers lacked control and engineers ended up writing custom traits and effects for specific cards ([Brian Cronin 2021, 12:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=725)).

The second is what you forget to put in data. Hinenzon argues that timing is essential in any narrative game and designers should control it, but in Sunshine Shuffle the timing of conversation, poker and pacing lived in float variables scattered across C# scripts, some tied to how long UI stayed hidden. Programmers had to step in to tune it, at a cost in iteration time ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 9:58](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=598)). If a parameter shapes the player's experience, it belongs where designers can reach it.

The third is deliberate: not everything should be configurable. Biskup fixes a middle layer of core RPG rules (attributes, dodge value, protection value) and never intended to let arbitrary rules be injected into Ultimate ADOM, because the more generic an engine gets, the more complicated it becomes. Knowing those rules lets the team store data directly in entities, making lookups and changes easier ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 2:22](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=142)).

**In practice:** put things (items, monsters, terrain, cards, encounters, text, tuning numbers and timings) in data; keep the core rules and the interpreter in well-tested code; and give data an escape hatch for the genuinely special case. Caves of Qud's is explicit: data can attach C# "parts" to objects when behaviour needs real code ([Ray 2023, 2:39](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=159)). Ultimate ADOM does the same by mapping names in JSON to C# classes, so a modder can drop in a new effect class (see the next section) ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 32:59](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1979)). When a card or item needs custom code, treat that as a sign that the data format is missing a concept, as Cronin's Vent example shows ([Brian Cronin 2021, 12:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=725)).

## Modelling entities: ECS, components and the alternatives

### Where ECS came from

An entity component system (ECS) splits a game object into an entity (an identity), components (data, sometimes with behaviour) and systems (logic that runs over entities with particular components). Nystrom traces it to real-time AAA games of the 1990s, whose game-object classes ran to around 20,000 lines mixing AI, physics, animation and rendering. Pulling each domain into its own component made the entity a bag of components, the game loop ran each domain as a separate phase, and storing each kind of component in a contiguous array avoided cache misses that can be two orders of magnitude slower, which mattered as RAM speed fell behind CPUs ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 3:48](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=228)).

### The debate: does it fit a roguelike?

Nystrom's position is that classic domain-split ECS is a poor fit for turn-based tile roguelikes. Their physics and graphics are trivial and nearly all the complexity is in AI, so splitting a monster by domain yields a lopsided result: useless animation and physics components and one AI component that does everything. When he polled his audience, only about three people had performance problems traced to cache misses ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 7:54](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=474)). Wanting ECS without those problems, he says, is like asking a doctor for a C-section when you are not pregnant.

Biskup is the enthusiastic counterweight. He had not heard of ECS until a conversation with Josh Ge of Cogmind at the previous Roguelike Celebration, and Ultimate ADOM adopted one, modified to handle very large numbers of entities ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 18:18](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1098)). But his ECS is not the pure version, in which an entity is only an ID, a component only data and a system all the behaviour. For roguelikes he disagrees with that: in Ultimate ADOM entities are both identifiers and data containers, components hold data plus simple related behaviour (a hit point component knows how to react to damage), and systems handle only complex, reusable logic. Because the game has a fixed core rule set, data can live in the entity; he reports better modularisation and easier modding ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 1:50](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=110)).

The two are less opposed than they look. Nystrom is rejecting the split by *domain* and the performance argument ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 7:54](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=474)); the benefits Biskup reports are modularisation and modding, not cache performance ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 1:50](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=110)). What the choice depends on is whether your game needs things to change what they are at runtime, which is where Biskup's examples are strongest ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 21:23](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1283)).

### What components buy

Biskup's demonstrations show composition doing things inheritance makes hard:

- **Soul swapping.** To swap the player's soul with an orc's, remove the UI-control component from the player and add it to the orc; because the systems already interpret the components, that is enough. He says this was impossible in ADOM and would have taken hundreds or even a thousand lines in ADOM 2 ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 19:40](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1180)).
- **Changing kind.** ADOM 2's object-oriented design made turning one type of thing into another very hard because they sat in different inheritance hierarchies. With components, a possessed player's lifeless body loses its "being" aspect and gains an item flag, so it can lie on the map or be picked up, though Biskup admits a complex item with equipment, slots and body parts raises its own interaction questions ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 21:23](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1283)).
- **Slots.** Ultimate ADOM's slots plug grouped features onto an entity as swappable sub-entities. They began so that alchemy could turn an iron sword into a mithril one by swapping the material slot, and were extended to race and profession, so a dwarven warrior gets a Dwarf slot and a Warrior slot whose components attach without explicit definition ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 15:21](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=921)).
- **Composed effects.** A battle axe of sharpness inherits from battleaxe and adds an "of sharpness" suffix slot whose triggered-effect component listens for the melee-damage event and runs a list of reusable effects; fire or paralysis could be added to the list. A reflection-based JSON parser maps names to C# classes, so a modder can add a new class implementing a one-method effect interface (actor, cause, target position, target) ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 32:59](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1979)). The amputation effect itself is about ten lines, because it delegates to shared systems: grafting picks and removes the body part, item management drops it, and a blood system handles bleeding ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 35:26](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=2126)).

Rich Wilson makes the same case for immersive sims in a sentence: component-based approaches help because you can say "this thing emits fire" and put that on whatever objects you want ([Rich Wilson 2021, 29:44](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1784)). Biskup also reports that an early Java ECS prototype ran a single level ten times the size of all ADOM's levels combined, with millions of entities, efficiently, though he doubts players want levels that big ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 29:15](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1755)).

### Lighter alternatives

Nystrom offers two patterns that get most of the composition benefit without a full ECS.

**Capability objects.** Instead of an item inheritance hierarchy, which breaks once you want a sword that shoots fireballs, Nystrom gives each item separate fields for capabilities such as attack, defence and use. A fireball-shooting sword or a shield that bashes is just a different mix. "Use" is itself a shallow, wide polymorphic hierarchy, the case where he thinks inheritance works well. He describes it as components split by capability rather than domain, it suits defining content in data files and building item kinds procedurally, and he uses the same idea for monster special moves ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 11:38](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=698)).

**Type objects.** Twenty goblins share most of their properties, so rather than storing that state in every monster, a single Breed instance holds it and each goblin points to it, keeping only its own position and health. Because Breed is effectively a metaclass, you can add features like a parent breed with your own inheritance rules. Nystrom uses the same pattern for tile types, item types and item modifiers ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 13:50](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=830)).

Biskup arrived at the same ideas from the ECS side. An ECS needs a typing mechanism, he says, because defining an orc as "having these 37 components with certain values" is crazy; Ultimate ADOM uses named entity templates with multiple inheritance, so an orc warrior or orc shaman still counts as an orc, and a few definitions cover 400 to 500 monsters needing 20 to 30 components each ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 9:51](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=591)). And since one orc warrior can be 30 to 40 entities (race, profession, body parts, items, materials), entities refer to a shared template for as long as they can and copy only changed data locally, flyweight-style. An uninjured orc warrior is an ID plus a template reference; a thousand of them cost little memory ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 12:04](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=724)). Breed objects and entity templates are the same answer to the same problem.

NetHack shows how far a small piece of data-driven polymorphism can go. Pepers describes how it maps each humanoid body part to an equivalent for each body plan: a jelly has a pseudopod for an arm and a dark spot for an eye, animals have forelimbs and claws. A body-part function takes the humanoid term and the creature and returns the right word, so a bear trap closing on your "foot" reads correctly for a polymorphed player or a steed, with exceptions such as sharks having skin rather than scales. Pepers called it her favourite technique: very specific output handled generically ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 13:35](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=815)).

### The costs

Composition creates combinations nobody designed. Biskup lists Ultimate ADOM's: mis-routed events let a player standing on a spider's severed part spin webs; a backpacked orc arm still holding a club gave a third melee attack; opening an animated door replaced the entity and lost its animation; a typing bug turned a sword made of iron into a material itself ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 35:58](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=2158)). Structural changes are expensive too: animating a wall into a living being means a tile that is a wall must also become a being, changing its type hierarchy at runtime, which he calls complex and wide-reaching and something to plan for if you want such transformations ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 13:57](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=837)).

**In practice:** if your game is turn-based and your monsters do not need to change kind, Nystrom's capability fields and type objects give you composition and shared data with little machinery ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 11:38](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=698); [Bob Nystrom 2018, 13:50](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=830)). If things must transform (possession, animation, transmutation), components and slots earn their cost, but budget for templates, event routing and a class of emergent bugs ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 9:51](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=591); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 35:58](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=2158)). Either way, choose granularity by capability, not by engine domain ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 7:54](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=474)).

## Turns, actions and events: where behaviour lives

Once entities are mostly data, the question is where the code that makes things happen should go. Two models dominate the talks, and several others are worth knowing.

### Actions: a turn as an object

Nystrom represents each turn as an Action object, applying the command pattern. Speed systems are the reason: a loop of "the hero moves, then every monster moves" cannot handle actors acting at different rates. His loop gives each actor energy according to its speed; when an actor crosses a threshold it is asked for an action, which the loop performs, iterating as consequences percolate. An action like walking, which may open a door or start an attack, carries a lot of code that would otherwise bloat the actor class, leaving actors as mostly data ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 17:18](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1038)).

> You can think of it as a first-class turn. — [Bob Nystrom 2018, 17:18](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1038)

Cronin's black box simulation (see the next section) uses a stricter version. Every state change goes through a self-contained, serialisable world command whose resolve function takes a world state, so there is no global state; a heal-once-per-turn command takes a target team and an amount. Commands never create or call other commands; shared logic goes into static helper functions, and serialised commands are how Inkbound's networking worked ([Brian Cronin 2024, 16:36](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=996)).

### Events: logic in listeners

Day's answer to Desktop Dungeons' fungal gods was to move all gameplay logic into handlers. Game objects only store state; handlers listen for events, change state and emit further events. A throw emits a throw event; the throw handler, if a potion hits an enemy, emits a quaff event; the potion handler emits begin-levitating; and a god handler can listen to all of these and approve or disapprove, so every god-specific line sits in one place ([Danny Day 2018, 5:33](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=333)). Each player input starts a cascade through an event queue, and the turn ends when every emitted event has percolated through: a grid click becomes a move event, the movement handler issues reveal events for new tiles, and a regeneration handler hears reveals and updates health and mana ([Danny Day 2018, 7:51](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=471)). What makes the system earn its keep, Day says, is that handlers can be added and removed at runtime: a damaged enemy gets its own regeneration handler, which listens for reveals and destroys itself once health is full, so nothing has to loop over every enemy asking whether it is hurt ([Danny Day 2018, 10:57](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=657)).

Biskup's Ultimate ADOM uses events in the same role. Its movement system knows nothing about solidity or spells; it fires events at six to eight phases (alter direction, bump interactions, leave old cell, enter new cell, finish), and any component on the entity or the map cell can intercept them. Confusion alters direction, bumping opens doors or attacks, a bear trap or glue blocks leaving, a cell spell deals damage on leaving, a force field blocks entry, and none of it is if-else code in the movement system ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 29:05](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=1745)). Components call systems directly for complex, reused operations like amputation, and everything else is event-driven. Biskup says the event routing was the hardest part to build, because of caching, performance and the fact that adding or removing a component changes the routes; once working, it is a stable base that decouples components ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 8:53](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=533)).

The convergence here is real: Nystrom, Day, Cronin and Biskup all pull behaviour out of the entity and into small, separately addressable units, whether called actions, handlers or commands.

### Costs and fixes

Events trade readability and predictability for flexibility, and the talks give specific remedies:

- **Ordering.** Desktop Dungeons keeps ordering deterministic with fixed handler priorities (god handlers sit high), and breaks event loops by splitting a handler into a high-priority and a low-priority half, where the low half can never issue an event the high half cares about. Day says the real problems were mismatches between UI and game state, not random ordering ([Danny Day 2018, 27:50](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1670)). Hades shows what happens when ordering is assumed not to matter: Lai describes trait systems that were supposed to be order-agnostic but were not, so a Dionysus poison fog combined with a certain shield instead detonated repeatedly ([Alice Lai 2021, 16:51](https://youtu.be/pXib0WTfLbI?t=1011)).
- **Readability.** To recover what decoupling hides, Desktop Dungeons has a verbose-events debug mode: break when a specific event is handled or passed between systems, print everything that happened to it, and step through the saved event log. Good event names keep it workable ([Danny Day 2018, 24:40](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1480)).
- **Performance.** Day is frank that dynamic event handlers are not performant, with cache misses guaranteed, which makes them a poor fit for real-time games. For turn-based games it is fine: early on the team logged thousands of events per frame without big drops, and the largest queue in Desktop Dungeons is around 50 events ([Danny Day 2018, 20:18](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1218)).

### Coroutines: for and against

Berman argues that a card-game rules engine should use the language's own coroutines, fibers or async rather than a homemade virtual machine, so that the code's call stack mirrors the game's logical call stack: when something receives damage, you should see a receive-damage function on the stack, which makes debugging far easier ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:05](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1265)). Cronin, from Monster Train, sees the downside. A coroutine keeps a timed sequence (animate, wait 0.8 seconds, resolve the death trigger, animate) readable in one place, which suits prototyping, but it bundles UI, input, sound and game logic together with no separation of concerns, and Monster Train ended up running its whole game loop as one giant coroutine ([Brian Cronin 2021, 6:39](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=399)). The difference is what goes in the coroutine: Berman is describing pure rule resolution; Cronin's trouble came from mixing presentation timing into it.

### Other shapes

Several narrower patterns solve particular problems:

- **One controller for everyone.** Leif Bloomquist's Commodore 64 multiplayer roguelike runs a Java server in a loose model-view-controller split where all entity actions, from players and monsters alike, pass through the same controller, so monsters interact with the world the same way players do ([Leif Bloomquist 2018, 11:06](https://youtu.be/Y0K-e83wYnQ?t=666)).
- **Priority queues for blocking events.** Sunshine Shuffle feeds dialogue and poker events as "chores" into one priority queue; blocking events like an all-in or a showdown get higher priority and lock out conversation until resolved, after which a marker returns to the conversation ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 7:16](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=436)).
- **Finite state machines.** Compton notes that locked and unlocked chests, alive and dead, and menu navigation are all finite state machines, and the interpreter is the hero: one director tracks state instead of every chest checking itself every frame ([Kate Compton 2016, 17:48](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=1068)).
- **A single mechanism.** Dustin Freeman's Spirit of the Ages expresses all AI as concerns, with no meta-controller: each entity is a bag of concerns, and a concern that wants control must raise its own probability, which may provoke reactions from others ([Dustin Freeman 2022, 24:43](https://youtu.be/RYZSdPuvta8?t=1483)).
- **Interpreters over reported actions.** Spencer Egart's ritual spells report every game action to an interpreter that tracks progress through each ritual's steps, tolerating a few intervening actions (taking out chalk before drawing) but timing out so a spell cannot fire by accident hours later; on completion it calls the game's existing spell system ([Spencer Egart 2019, 11:15](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=675)).
- **Indexed triggers.** Mark Johnson stores generated riddle solutions as tuples keyed by action type, then exact coordinates and optional modifiers, indexed per map zone, so on each action only that zone's triggers with a matching action type are examined. His example is holding up a sword with particular properties at specific coordinates at night under a full moon ([Mark Johnson 2023, 27:05](https://youtu.be/RDWt6RGN9wM?t=1625)).

### Choosing

Use **actions or commands** when you need a clean unit of turn, for speed systems, undo, replays or networking ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 17:18](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=1038); [Brian Cronin 2024, 16:36](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=996)). Use **events** when many independent rules (gods, traps, curses, mods) need to react to the same moments without knowing about each other, and pay for it with explicit priorities and an event log ([Danny Day 2018, 5:33](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=333); [Danny Day 2018, 27:50](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1670); [Danny Day 2018, 24:40](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1480)). Use **coroutines** for rule resolution whose call stack you want to read in the debugger, but keep presentation timing out of them ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:05](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1265); [Brian Cronin 2021, 6:39](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=399)). The models combine: Ultimate ADOM calls systems directly for heavy operations and routes everything else as events ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 8:53](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=533)).

## Isolate the simulation: state, logic and presentation

### The black box

Several talks arrive independently at the same architecture: a simulation that knows nothing about the screen. Cronin calls it the black box sim, and its most important principle is strict separation of four things. Static data (a tank definition) does not change and is loaded from disk or the network; state (ten tank instances with different HP) lives in memory; logic, driven by the player or the system, acts on state; and presentation (UI, animation, sound) tells the player what happened. The interfaces between them should be strict and clear ([Brian Cronin 2024, 8:54](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=534)).

> Strict separation of data from state, logic, and presentation. — [Brian Cronin 2024, 8:54](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=534)

After Monster Train, Cronin advocated an isolated world state modified only by a world engine that processes commands and outputs world state changes, to which presentation systems such as sound, animation and achievements subscribe. Commands do not map one-to-one to changes: damage may or may not cause a death. He likens it to model-view-controller, with game objects becoming a view into the state that never needs to touch engine code ([Brian Cronin 2021, 21:51](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1311)).

The cost of not doing this is clearest in ADOM. Biskup calls its biggest technical problem a user interface that is not separated from game logic but runs through all the code, which makes a viable mobile version practically impossible; the team tried and concluded it was too hard, which motivated a new architecture ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=564)). Ultimate ADOM's answer runs the engine on a separate thread from the Unity UI. Because two threads invite trouble, such as the UI showing damage on an orc the engine has already killed, the engine sends minimal "UI signals" carrying the data the renderer needs, plus a few specifically synchronised queries; Biskup found little data actually needs to cross ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 7:38](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=458)).

### The techniques

The details converge across talks:

- **One serialisable state.** Cronin keeps all simulation state, including the random number generator, in a single highly serialisable world-state structure, mostly integers keyed by entity, with a read-only interface. He avoids floating point himself ([Brian Cronin 2024, 13:31](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=811)).
- **One-way control.** Input and UI tell the sim what the player wants; the sim never calls back up into them. Cronin compares the sim to an API with strictly formatted inputs and outputs, and says the principles come from 16 years of building shoddy gameplay architecture ([Brian Cronin 2024, 10:31](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=631)).
- **Presentation reads only change records.** World commands emit world-state-change records carrying everything presentation needs (unit healed, previous and new HP), which drive VFX, animation and sound and are never read inside the sim. Because commands resolve instantly, anything that needs animating must be fully described in a state change ([Brian Cronin 2024, 20:11](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1211)).
- **UI last.** Desktop Dungeons separated UI from logic within its event system by giving UI handlers the lowest priority, so they see each event only after every game handler has modified it; otherwise the UI might show experience gained before an angry god docked some. The team also added the ability to inject events mid-queue, after the current event or at the end, such as a UI refresh ([Danny Day 2018, 13:22](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=802)).
- **State as values.** Lachlan Kingsford, using Monte Carlo tree search to balance games, says the game state should be held in memory with actions as pure functions that return a new state without side effects, so many hypothetical moves can be computed quickly; pure functions also let you replay from any point for fuzzing ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 9:51](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=591)). Berman recommends storing state in an arena allocator such as Cap'n Proto so it can be copied and sent as byte buffers for multiplayer and for AI that copies state; anyone who has written "entity" in their codebase, he says, has already reinvented one ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:42](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1302)).
- **Output as data.** Kovach's relational engine takes the idea to its end: rules map game facts into output relations (DOM nodes or grid glyphs) that a small driver outside the engine interprets, and mutable slots like equipment are modelled by aggregating equip and unequip events ([Scott Kovach 2019, 31:27](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=1887)).

### The payoffs

The benefits are the ones Cronin listed at the end of the chapter's first section ([Brian Cronin 2024, 3:03](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=183)), and the talks give concrete cases. Because Inkbound's sim was isolated, its game server ran it as a pure C# program without Unity at all, efficiently on Amazon EC2; Cronin adds that an isolated sim could even be written in a different language from the engine ([Brian Cronin 2024, 12:18](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=738)). An isolated state is far easier to serialise for saves and networking, and Monster Train missed features because it lacked one: server-side run verification against cheating and mid-battle saves were both too much work; snapshots could also have supported rollback or run history ([Brian Cronin 2021, 23:22](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1402)). Previews need a deterministic simulation, which Cronin says must be designed in from the start, because random number generation and cross-platform floating point both break it. Monster Train did not do that, so sound effects and warnings had to be special-cased for preview mode throughout its coroutine loop ([Brian Cronin 2021, 8:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=486)). The sections on presentation and on saves, replays and networking below follow these payoffs through in detail.

The same lesson comes from Berman: without designing state for copying up front, he faced a years-old card base that could not easily support multiplayer or a textbook AI, requiring months of rewriting ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:42](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1302)). Berman, Cronin and Biskup each found that this separation is far cheaper at the start than later ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:42](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1302); [Brian Cronin 2021, 8:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=486); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=564)).

### Retrofitting, and living with coupling

None of the talks offers a painless retrofit. Biskup's experience with ADOM is that it may be impossible, and his route was a new engine, though he credits the graphical interface layer the team used for teaching them to separate engine from graphics cleanly ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=564)). Day's UI-last priority shows a smaller step that works inside an existing event system ([Danny Day 2018, 13:22](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=802)). If you must keep a coupled codebase for now, Cronin's advice from Monster Train is to log extensively, with filterable categories such as gameplay and audio; that was the main way the team followed its callback chains, and he now advocates not using callbacks at all ([Brian Cronin 2021, 25:41](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1541)).

## Presenting a turn-based world: animation, timing and text

Once the simulation is a black box that takes commands and emits state changes, something still has to show the player what happened. That presentation layer has two jobs in a roguelike: turn instantaneous rule resolution into motion the player can follow, and turn game state into readable sentences. Both go best when the presentation only ever reads from the simulation and never feeds back into it ([Brian Cronin 2024, 22:16](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1336)).

### Time lives in the presentation, not the simulation

Cronin states the rule plainly for his black-box simulation: it is "a computing machine" with no concept of time or animation. Players need animation to understand what happened, so the presentation layer takes the emitted state changes and sequences them over time (the card play, then the unit move, then the sword swing), one way only. By the time the animations play, the simulation has finished and the commands and changes are gone; the animations are self-sufficient. Cronin admits he is not fully happy with his own animation side ([Brian Cronin 2024, 22:16](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1336)).

The hard part is what that sequencing has to respect. Jeremiah Reid calls synchronising animations with the logical order of simultaneous turn events the hardest part of juicing a roguelike. If every animation simply plays out at once, a monster can visibly step away before the arrow fired at it has landed. He did not attempt it for his talk's prototype, and such glitches remain in Golden Krone Hotel because scheduling animations is a lot of work ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 27:58](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1678)). Put Cronin and Reid together and the requirement is clear: the presentation needs the simulation's changes in order, with enough structure to know which ones must wait for which. A flat list of "things that moved" is not enough.

### Techniques for scheduling animation

- **Scale everything by elapsed time, then lie about time.** Reid scales every animation by the frame's elapsed time, so a skipped frame means the next frame animates twice as far and choppy frame rates smooth out. Once every animation uses that clock, one global time multiplier can slow everything down to inspect motion that looks wrong, slow it for drama, or speed it up so animation never blocks the player ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 12:45](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=765)).
- **Compose effects from atoms in blocking and concurrent lists.** Thomas Robertson builds procedural super attacks from small atomic effects held in a list that ticks and draws each atom and removes it when it finishes. Atoms can spawn atoms, so a projectile creates an explosion when it arrives, which makes chaining flexible ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 2:49](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=169)). He keeps two lists, a blocking list whose atoms play one after another and a concurrent list whose atoms play at once, because complex attacks need both; in his code an atom can carry child atoms that move into the concurrent list when it finishes, so they all start together ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 5:10](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=310)). This is a small, general answer to Reid's ordering problem: "the arrow lands, then the monster moves" is a blocking sequence, and the explosion's particles are concurrent children.
- **Use a fixed timer when you need exact frames.** Patrick Devine, recreating NES Tetris in a terminal, adds a fixed 60-frames-per-second timer to the clear-update-draw loop so every frame matches the original; he notes other approaches suit sprites, but for blocky terminal movement a timer works best ([Patrick Devine 2019, 5:38](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=338)).
- **Let data draw itself while prototyping.** Robertson's prototyping approach declares game data as "smart variables" with limits and lists that can draw themselves into any screen rectangle. The main loop just asks the data to draw itself; inventories lay themselves out, and drag bars let him tune values such as movement speed live. It is a developer tool rather than player-facing UI, and he says it gets you about 80% of the way ([Thomas Robertson et al. 2017, 2:06](https://youtu.be/H6fPIhLoA1Y?t=126)).

### Text is presentation too

A roguelike tells much of its story in generated sentences, and the same principle applies: generate text from the state, do not hand-write it beside the state.

NetHack shows the small version. It wraps message output in a function named `You`, so that the many messages phrased as "You feel hungry" read as plain English in the source; Pepers calls this clever naming that hides the formatting cruft around the underlying print call ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 14:36](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=876)).

Caves of Qud shows the large version, and what it costs to retrofit. Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang describe the localisation rebuild:

- **Replacers instead of a replace loop.** The original templating ran a text replace for every possible placeholder over every string. That was fine with about 20 replacers, worse with 200 and poor with a thousand. The new system matches a placeholder such as `subject.direction` to a function named `Direction` marked with a C# attribute, which gives constant-time lookup and lets modders add replacers without editing one giant function ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:33:50](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5630)).
- **Typed arguments.** At 1.0 the templating was used reliably only in conversations and object descriptions, with inconsistent grammar helpers elsewhere. For localisation the replacers had to accept rich arguments (factions, numbers, calendars, historic entities, lists, booleans) as typed method parameters, with argument types detected at runtime to pick the right replacer. The example shows why: "the gnu sees a snapjaw to its north and stops grazing" and "you see a snapjaw to the north and stop grazing" differ in both conjugation and articles ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:36:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5813)).
- **Wrap every string with context for translators.** Following GNU gettext, every translatable string is wrapped in a call, `_S` for static strings and `_T` for templates, whose first argument is a human-readable context such as "inventory take from direction". The context is exported to the translators' file but never shown in game, which matters because the templates themselves are hard to read. `_T` returns a chainable builder for arguments, including some English does not use but other languages need ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:40:11](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6011)).
- **Extract strings from the source mechanically.** The team parses its C# with Microsoft's Roslyn analyzers, collecting every `_T` and `_S` call with its context, file and line into a strings XML table of about 6,000 lines so far. Exported example files prefix every value with a right-pointing triangle, which proved an unexpectedly useful marker of what still needs translating; XML game data goes out through the modding framework's merge support, with C# attributes marking fields that hold display text ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:47:35](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6455)).

What is still missing is telling. Translators mostly work in raw XML with no in-game view of a string in its context, and the team calls tooling one of its big unknowns; the same tool would help English authors write procedural templates ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:59:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=7194)).

**In practice:** keep presentation one-way. Have the simulation emit ordered changes and let an animation scheduler with blocking and concurrent tracks play them back on its own clock, with a global speed multiplier for debugging and for impatient players ([Brian Cronin 2024, 22:16](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1336); [Thomas Robertson 2021, 5:10](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=310); [Jeremiah Reid 2021, 12:45](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=765)). Treat text the same way: build sentences from typed game data through named, discoverable template functions, wrap every player-facing string so it can be extracted, and give writers a way to see a template rendered in context ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:33:50](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=5630); [Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:47:35](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6455); [Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:59:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=7194)).

## Saves, determinism, replays and networking

Saving a game, replaying it, undoing a move, verifying a run on a server and playing it over a network look like five features. The talks treat them as one question: can you serialise the game's state and the changes to it, and replay those changes deterministically? If you can, each feature is a short step ([Brian Cronin 2024, 25:33](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1533)). If you cannot, each is a separate, painful retrofit.

### Serialise the changes, not just the state

Day describes the most striking payoff. Desktop Dungeons stores save games as serialised strings of handled events, such as "player built a building", replayed on load. When content is removed, an event with no handler simply fizzles, and because only handled events are stored, saves prune themselves. Across two and a half years of early access players never needed a progress reset; a save-size bug surfaced only three years in, which a reset at release would have hidden ([Danny Day 2018, 18:52](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1132)). The same stream gives replays almost for free, and Day regrets not building gameplay replays from the start, because retrofitting them proved too complicated. For undo he recommends keeping a stack of game-state snapshots, perhaps one every 20 events, and replaying inputs from the nearest one, rather than making every event reversible, which gets complicated with long chains ([Danny Day 2018, 22:21](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1341)).

Cronin reaches the same place from the other direction. With all world state in one structure, save and load is serialising that structure, networking is syncing world commands, and a replay is the initial state plus the commands, or just the state changes. Animation and player input usually break determinism, but in his design they sit outside the simulation as its outputs and inputs. Inkbound synchronised world commands over very little bandwidth, and a bug can be reproduced by checking out the matching git commit and running the simulation until the same error appears ([Brian Cronin 2024, 25:33](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1533)).

> You can serialize the world commands and the initial world state to regenerate the replay. — [Brian Cronin 2024, 25:33](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1533)

### Store only what generation cannot recreate

A procedurally generated world can be regenerated from its seed, so the save need only hold the difference. Greg L describes a PICO-8 game with generated stone and trees that remembers what you dug out across reloads: at generation it records every destructible object, and the save packs one destroyed-or-not bit per object as tightly as possible. He suggests the approach for web games, online saves and huge maps ([Greg L 2026, 9:08](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=548)). The idea is old. Aaron A. Reed describes how Star Trek (1971) stored each quadrant of its 8x8 galaxy only as a three-digit count of Klingons, starbases and stars; the code the player learned to read was the literal in-memory representation, and positions were re-randomised on entry, a lossy compression players rarely noticed and could read as Klingons moving ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 12:55](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=775)). For simulations that change every cell, Scott Anderson suggests storing falling-sand worlds sparsely, with homogeneous chunks as a single value, per-chunk bit depths of 1, 4 or 8, and possibly HashLife-style memoisation ("hash sand"), though he has not seen it tried ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:37:44](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16664)).

### What goes wrong: the raw-struct save

The opposite approach is to write memory structures straight to disk. Russ, who ran a patched NetHack server at RIT, explains that in NetHack (and similarly Rogue) changing the player structure or many other parts of the source breaks every existing save and bones file, and that this was one of the biggest limits on what they could change on a live server ([Tariq et al. 2016, 11:36](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=696)). His fix shows how expensive retrofitting is: to get forward-compatible JSON saves from C, which lacks introspection, he serialised the structs by having the program debug itself, the subject of a master's thesis and about a year of work ([Tariq et al. 2016, 12:22](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=742)).

### Networking is a spectrum; pick the cheapest point

Adrian Zeyfang lays out the options for Crypt of the NecroDancer's multiplayer. Authoritative-server state replication sends inputs to a server that propagates updates, so a keypress shows only after a round trip. Deterministic lockstep relays inputs and simulates locally, which works only if the simulation has no outside dependencies or unshared randomness, but it is also called "delay netcode" because inputs still wait for the round trip. For a rhythm game, both lags were unacceptable ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 3:03](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=183)). So the team built rollback: run local inputs at once, snapshot the full game state every tick (globals, RNG seeds, tiles, positions, health, timers, items), and when a late remote input arrives, return to the past turn, insert it and fast-forward. Zeyfang describes it as an undo/redo system for the entire game, in effect a save/load system that must be extremely fast because it runs many times a second ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 4:30](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=270)).

The details show where rollback gets hard. A frame-indexed action buffer was mostly empty, so they keyed it by beat number, which broke when the beat-free Bard character could act at any time: a fast Bard built a lead, a rhythm player's input landed far behind it, and the resulting massive rollbacks caused performance problems and teleporting objects ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 10:02](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=602)). The fix was a sparse map keyed by time-derived turn IDs. Rhythm players snap to beat-aligned IDs so simultaneous beats share one ID; Bard's IDs come straight from the timestamp; Bolt, at double tempo, gets twice as many IDs and acts alone on off-beats; an out-of-order arrival shifts later actions and rolls back to weave the new one in ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 10:29](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=629)). And some state must stay out of rollback entirely: beat-timing judgement is fully client-authoritative and kept out of snapshots, so network trouble can never make a player miss a beat ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 14:31](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=871)).

Tyriq Plummer is the counterweight. Inspired by Zeyfang's talk, he spent two months failing to implement rollback for Scrubbin' Trubble before concluding it is a specific technology for a specific subset of games, and that most online games, turn-based ones especially, do not need it ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 8:47](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=527)). He switched to lockstep: clients send actions to the server, wait for confirmation, then simulate locally, so the server never sends game state but the game must be strictly deterministic. The internet turned out faster than he expected for this ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 9:10](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=550)). Anderson gives the same advice for falling-sand multiplayer: network inputs, not state, keep the simulation including its RNG deterministic, and choose lockstep or rollback as fighting and RTS games do; rollback re-simulation is expensive for sand, lockstep's latency may suit a sandbox, and full state sync would need something like lossless video compression ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:38:44](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16724)).

The choice depends on what latency your game can tolerate. NecroDancer's rhythm cannot wait a round trip; a turn-based game usually can, and lockstep then costs far less. At the light end, the Delve Bros' Stream Heist viewer interface is a plain REST web app polled once a second. It only pretends to be synchronous, which does not matter when Twitch already adds several seconds of delay ([The Delve Bros 2020, 39:23](https://youtu.be/4jNMv79Xb6A?t=2363)). Networking also changes how you ship: Bloomquist notes that because his multiplayer roguelike is networked, every player, including those on a Commodore 64, always plays the latest version, which lets him introduce features and tweak them by player response ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 8:16](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=496)).

### Replays as verification and as explanation

A deterministic replay can check that a run is honest. For the 2017 MIT Mystery Hunt, whose solvers assume page source and protocols may be part of the puzzle, Colin Liotta ran a puzzle roguelike client-side without trusting the client: on reaching the stairs, the client sent its exact keypress sequence, the server replayed it with identical code, and only a winning replay returned the next level's URL; a failure earned a one-minute timeout ([Colin Liotta 2018, 7:08](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=428)). He wrote it in JavaScript precisely so the same simulation code could run on client and server, and recommends rot.js for web roguelikes ([Colin Liotta 2018, 7:43](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=463)).

Replays also explain. Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup keeps frame-by-frame ttyrec recordings of every online game. Alan Malloy used one to show a player how two stacked damage multipliers took them from 230 health to dead in one turn, and another player used a replay to prove magic mapping had failed in the Realm of Zot, exposing a real bug Malloy would otherwise have closed as unreproducible ([Alan Malloy 2017, 12:08](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=728)). Seeds serve the same purpose for generation: Brian Walker built Brogue's seed feature so players could send him seeds for one-in-ten-thousand level-generation bugs that he could then step through, and it later became the basis of seed contests where everyone plays the same levels ([Brian Walker 2018, 31:02](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1862)).

**In practice:** keep the simulation deterministic, with its RNG inside the state, and record the initial state (or seed) plus the stream of commands or events. Saves, replays, bug reproduction, server-side verification and lockstep networking all fall out of that ([Brian Cronin 2024, 25:33](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1533); [Danny Day 2018, 22:21](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1341); [Colin Liotta 2018, 7:08](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=428); [Tyriq Plummer 2025, 9:10](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=550)). Avoid raw memory dumps as a save format ([Tariq et al. 2016, 11:36](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=696)). Reach for rollback only if your game cannot tolerate a round trip of input lag, and keep anything that must never be rolled back, such as rhythm judgement, out of the snapshot ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 8:47](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=527); [Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 14:31](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=871)).

## Designing for modders

A data-driven, event-driven architecture is most of a mod system already. The question the talks raise is whether you treat modding as a design goal from the start or bolt it on later, and their answer is consistent.

### Plan for it early

Moromisato, who built Transcendence's mod system, reports hearing the same advice from Brian Bucklew of Caves of Qud and from the Dwarf Fortress developers: plan for modding from the start, because it is much harder to retrofit. You need not have it worked out, only put in some hooks and know the basic architecture ([George Moromisato 2022, 18:48](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1128)). Matt Ritchie built Axu that way, with a mod system that gives modders the same tools he has, and frames it as building broadly, layer by layer like a pyramid rather than a tall tower that falls over ([Matt Ritchie 2017, 5:08](https://youtu.be/KKwgKTbiEY0?t=308)). Dylan Gedig offers the hindsight version: Peglin builds each orb or relic from reusable Unity components, which made the team's own experimentation fast but did not make the game easy for outside modders, and he says he would now set it up for modding from the start ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 28:19](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1699)). Peglin's case is a useful warning that a component architecture convenient for the team is not automatically a mod system.

### From forks to hooks

Roguelikes were traditionally modded by forking the source. NetHack and its many variants came about that way, adding creatures and items as new code. Moromisato notes that forking is easy for the developer (just open the source), but it gets harder as games grow, limits modding to expert programmers, and forks cannot be combined ([George Moromisato 2022, 5:56](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=356)).

Scripting hooks fix the combination problem. In Moromisato's example, the attack code rolls damage, then calls mod events such as `onAttack` and `onDefend` with the attacker, defender and damage before hit points are decremented. A fireball mod handles `onAttack`, a magic-creature mod handles `onDefend`, and when both are loaded both run, with neither author needing to know about the other. He names Caves of Qud and Transcendence as using scripting like this ([George Moromisato 2022, 15:11](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=911)). This is the way out of the unfillable interaction matrix described at the start of the chapter, where no one decided what one mod's fireball did to another mod's creature ([George Moromisato 2022, 5:26](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=326)).

> If they are both in the same game we call both events and it work and neither mod/programmer has to worry about them being combined. — [George Moromisato 2022, 15:11](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=911)

### What it costs

Hooks multiply. In Transcendence, player requests extended buff events from the attacker to the attacker's items, allies and allies' items. And because mods run code, they exercise the engine harder than your own content does: Moromisato gets many crash reports that turn out to be mods doing unexpected things, and says any engine bug will be found by mods ([George Moromisato 2022, 16:53](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1013)).

Data-only modding has its own limits, which Ray describes from Caves of Qud's XML. Reusing a part works only when its boundaries match the change the modder wants. Rocket boots' jumping and fire trail are one part, so a modder who wants only the fire trail must drop into C# ([Ray 2023, 9:25](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=565)). Push the other way, making the data more expressive, and you hit a tension between power and comprehensibility: Ray argues Qud's XML effectively is a programming language, if a much simpler one than C#, and conditional behaviour based on other mods or game state is still harder than it could be ([Ray 2023, 9:46](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=586)). That tension is the subject of the next section.

### Moromisato's practical rules

- **Dogfood the system.** Build your own first-party content with your mod system. All of Transcendence's content is implemented in it; this speeds content creation, exercises the system so modders hit fewer gaps, and features modders ask for often turn out useful for official content ([George Moromisato 2022, 19:45](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1185)).
- **Version the API from day one.** Require every mod to declare the API version it was built against, so the engine can switch to old behaviour when an update changes things. You cannot add this later, because you cannot go back in time once you change the API; Transcendence does modify behaviour by mod version, which is expensive but sometimes worth it ([George Moromisato 2022, 25:49](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1549)).
- **Generate the documentation from the code.** Embed each script function's documentation in the code that registers it, make it required to compile, and generate the docs. Moromisato wishes Transcendence had started that way; its players diff the generated function lists between versions to update a community wiki ([George Moromisato 2022, 27:21](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1641)).

Everest Pipkin takes the idea of permission further. Pipkin works in the browser because its surface is only skin deep: players can view source, so the game's logic becomes transparent, readable and permissible to touch ([Everest Pipkin 2023, 25:24](https://youtu.be/O78uYtUZKYs?t=1524)). That is a design stance as well as a technical one: a game whose workings are open invites players to look underneath.

## Little languages: writing rules in a language built for them

Compton's provocation to roguelike developers is that you have probably already written a programming language. Any file your program uses to control its flow, including a homemade save or data format, is one, and it reflects what your game needs and is about; it may have first-class constructs for things only your game has, such as the number of eggs you hold ([Kate Compton 2020, 8:51](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=531)). The previous section's Caves of Qud XML is an example. Since you will have a language anyway, the talks argue you should design or choose it on purpose.

### Why a language for the domain
