Kovach's argument is about where effort goes. General-purpose programming carries incidental chores: package management, dependency versions, learning APIs, choosing data structures. The hard problems are making rules fun, fair and easy to learn and making interfaces that communicate. Choosing or designing a domain-specific language (DSL), a language built for one kind of problem, shifts effort from the first kind to the second ([Scott Kovach 2019, 2:56](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=176)). Compton adds that designing a DSL is also a way of thinking about a genre: you ask what its unit operations are and which ones you cannot express well in Python, as she did with Tracery, Tracery 2, Chancery and the speculative idle-game language Greenery ([Kate Compton 2020, 8:24](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=504)). Reed makes the case for writers: procedural text authors should get languages that feel like writing a manuscript, not wrangling a database. 18 Cadence let him write paragraphs tagged with a year and a location, Subcutanean used a simple DSL for text alternatives, and he credits a natural-language programming language with helping him finish Blue Lacuna ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 22:12](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1332)).

> Give the writer the best tools to write. Even if the writer is yourself. — [Aaron A. Reed 2020, 22:12](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1332)

### Families of rule languages

**Relational rules.** In Kovach's relational game language, the whole world state is a collection of typed facts such as `monster(m)`, `position(p)`, `adjacent(p1,p2)` and `at(m,p)`. Input and output are facts too: keypresses are transcribed into facts each loop, and queries join facts that share variables, for instance to find every pair of adjacent monsters ([Scott Kovach 2019, 14:57](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=897)). Logic rules derive new facts from queries and play the role of functions: "touching" from adjacency, "alive" from HP above zero, which stops being true by itself when HP hits zero, and reachability from just two recursive rules (adjacent implies reachable; adjacent plus reachable implies reachable), which settle whether a path exists though not the optimal A* path ([Scott Kovach 2019, 24:16](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=1456)). Because every fact exists only because some rule fired, you can ask of anything on screen why it is there and trace the chain back through time, which Kovach suggests helps both debugging and players who want to peel back the layers ([Scott Kovach 2019, 29:16](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=1756)).

Kovach points to two existing languages in this spirit. Stephen Lavelle's PuzzleScript expresses Sokoban's whole push mechanic as one pattern-to-consequence rule, and reversing its arrows yields a pull; the language is useless for general tasks but its whole execution model fits on one slide, which gives designers a simple mental model ([Scott Kovach 2019, 4:26](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=266)). Inform 7 lets interactive fiction authors write state and rules in near-natural English, for example defining a container as bursting when its contents outweigh its breaking strain, a definition that is itself a rule updating the world whenever it holds ([Scott Kovach 2019, 8:49](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=529)).

**Tile rewriting.** Seth Cooper's TRBT represents a grid game's whole state as a layered 2D board of tiles and every change as a visual rewrite of one tile pattern into another. Moving is rewriting player-plus-blank into blank-plus-player; placing a room is rewriting a rectangle of solid tiles into empty space; winning is matching a gem pattern ([Seth Cooper 2025, 2:04](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=124)). Behaviour trees, normally used for agent AI, control the logic of the whole game: order, loop-until-fail, any-order and player-choice nodes over rewrites. A minimal game fills the board, carves a room, places the player and exit, then loops a player node until a gem appears ([Seth Cooper 2025, 2:39](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=159)). Hidden state lives in extra layers: in Cooper's roguelike Trogue, underscore-tagged tiles visible only in a debug view sit under patrolling snakes to record their heading and whether they moved this turn ([Seth Cooper 2025, 8:26](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=506)).

**Effect graphs.** As an answer to the dependent, scaling card effects that defeated Monster Train's effect scripts (see "Where data stops"), Cronin proposes representing its card effects as a DSL of control-flow nodes and parameter nodes. Awoken Rail Spike becomes draw, upgrade and consume nodes fed by a parameter such as energy spent; changing it to draw one card per card in the discard pile, or doubling it with a multiplier node, is trivial rewiring. Designers get leverage over how effects resolve, and programmers write small, simple nodes ([Brian Cronin 2021, 15:28](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=928)).

### What makes a little language polite

Compton's talk is a design guide for languages built by people without a programming-language degree. Her first point is that a language is not its syntax but an ecosystem: programs (a Tracery grammar, a Stardew Valley config file), parsers, engines, IDEs, specifications, tools and the people who control each part ([Kate Compton 2020, 18:11](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1091)). What creators care about most are informal properties: is it easy to write, can you remember what a program does after writing it, can you use it in strange places, does it run on your device. Lua, made for Brazilian power plants and now in Roblox, is her example of a language that runs anywhere ([Kate Compton 2020, 19:00](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1140)). From there she lists what a polite ecosystem does:

- **Scaffold the user.** Show the available parts, offer completion, colouring and auto-indent, so people know what to do and when they have done it right, unlike a blank vi buffer ([Kate Compton 2020, 20:49](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1249)).
- **Offer a structure editor.** In an editor like Scratch only valid pieces snap together, so beginners cannot produce an error and can learn about errors later ([Kate Compton 2020, 21:12](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1272)).
- **Make syntax unfoldable.** HTML and Tracery let a beginner start with plain text and unfold more syntax step by step; many Tracery users only ever write hashtags. Compton says Caves of Qud's data is not currently very unfolded ([Kate Compton 2020, 21:45](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1305)).
- **Embed safely.** A polite language can squeeze in anywhere and run user-provided code safely; base Tracery is small enough that students port it to C, and Cheap Bots Done Quick relies on Tracery being mostly safe ([Kate Compton 2020, 23:21](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1401)).
- **Separate engine from tools.** Breaking Tracery's engine out of its parser and tools let George Buckenham build Cheap Bots Done Quick on it; Compton says most of the many tools she built were never that useful ([Kate Compton 2020, 24:26](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1466)). Her chatbot language Chancery went wrong the other way: IDE, simulator and visualisations were bundled too tightly for anyone to pull out just the simulator, so she split it ([Kate Compton 2020, 27:23](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1643)).
- **Model the syntax explicitly.** Railroad diagrams describe what a language's syntax is and are a step toward a specification, though hers for Tracery is unfinished because she keeps iterating on the diagrams ([Kate Compton 2020, 24:55](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1495)).

Read against the modding section, these are also guidelines for mod data: Ray's power-versus-comprehensibility tension is what unfoldable syntax and scaffolding are meant to ease.

### Declarative tools you already have

You do not have to build a language to get some of these benefits. Pagnutti, whose two-table state machine for a Slay the Spire enemy appears in the content-as-data section, set out to write a game simulation as a single SQL query, and says he also simulates games in nothing but Google Sheets ([Johnathan Pagnutti 2025, 13:27](https://youtu.be/Uf34SbuWIos?t=807)). He simulates Slay the Spire enemy behaviour with a recursive common table expression in SQLite: a seed step loads the start state, and a recursive step joins the transitions and states tables to append each possible next move. Each row tracks round, move trace, current state, running probability (the product of transition probabilities, starting at 1 because the first move is forced) and running damage, block and strength; by round three there are five possible traces. He notes recursive CTEs may not be standard SQL ([Johnathan Pagnutti 2025, 9:49](https://youtu.be/Uf34SbuWIos?t=589)).

Tyler Robertson goes further and runs games inside Google Sheets. The core tricks:

- **State through self-reference.** Turn on iterative calculation with a maximum of one iteration, and a cell can reference itself; with a checkbox as input, "if checked, increment my value, else keep it" becomes a counter, and each checkbox becomes a controller button ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 6:05](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=365)).
- **Event detection from calculation order.** Sheets compute left to right, top to bottom, so a pair of helper formulas, one that fires when the checkbox and its partner disagree and one that then copies the checkbox, can tell which checkbox was clicked most recently. Robertson says this took him about a year to understand ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 7:00](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=420)).
- **Rendering by rule.** Conditional formatting colours cells from rules, so tile types become numbers whose colour lives in one place; his pixel-accurate Mario 1-1 used about 90,000 cells, and recolouring the sky meant editing one rule ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 3:28](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=208)).
- **A roguelike in cells.** The map is text of dots (walkable) and pound signs (walls); a regex formula renders the player or the map tile, extra formulas check the target cell before moving, edge formulas shift when the player passes the screen centre to make a following camera, and a VLOOKUP can swap characters for emoji tiles ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 9:10](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=550)).

The same techniques extend to Snake, checkers, chess, text adventures and even slow 3D rendering; his turn-based strategy game took a month and had cells with 200 nested IF functions ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 12:25](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=745)), which shows both the reach of the approach and where it stops being comfortable. Adrian Herbez found a similar limit in OpenSCAD, the code-driven CAD modeller he uses to generate 3D-printable roguelike pieces: its variables are all constants, which makes substantial logic painful, so he generates the data in JavaScript and feeds it in ([Adrian Herbez 2019, 7:48](https://youtu.be/cGvig1f68Tg?t=468)).

### The cost of a new way of thinking

Kovach frames choosing a language like choosing a roguelike conduct, a self-imposed restriction like never equipping items. C's manual memory, Haskell's lack of mutable state and APL's terseness make some easy things hard but force new ways of thinking, and his relational language deliberately has no functions, no local state, no control flow and one data type ([Scott Kovach 2019, 13:18](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=798)). Cooper's experience shows the bill for that. In a tile rewrite language tiles have no identity, so even the player is just an emoji that any rule can match, and a rewrite involving the player tile applies to every player tile on the board. His small user study suggested this requires a different way of thinking about program structure than an object-oriented player entity ([Seth Cooper 2025, 15:54](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=954)). A little language pays off when its constraints match your game's problem closely enough that the new way of thinking is the design thinking you needed to do anyway; when they do not, you are paying to learn a conduct that does not help you win.

## Tools that keep designers iterating

The architecture above decides what the game can do; tools decide how quickly a team can find out whether it is any good. The useful way to judge a tool is by its turnaround: how long between making a change and seeing what it does?

### Turnaround is the measure

Two talks from very different corners of the field arrive at the same rule. JP LeBreton, who built the ASCII art and game tool Playscii, borrows the idea of *liveness* from Bret Victor: tighten feedback loops, make hidden things visible, and cut out the compile, reboot and reload steps between an action and its result. He contrasts it with waiting hours for a Quake or Half-Life map to recompile, and he asks of every action in his tool what its turnaround time is ([JP LeBreton 2019, 11:34](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=694)). Leigh Alexander, coming from generative writing, reaches the same conclusion for content: you cannot tell how a piece of generative text performs by reading it in a spreadsheet, so the spreadsheet has to feed a running instance of the game with near-zero latency, without full builds or code. She credits the writing awards for Reigns: Her Majesty to a toolset that let her, a non-technical designer, work exactly that way ([Leigh Alexander 2023, 29:49](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1789)).

> If you want to do anything good from a content standpoint with spreadsheets and generative tech you need to prioritize minimizing the latency. — [Leigh Alexander 2023, 29:49](https://youtu.be/NjYS8XmeaiY?t=1789)

LeBreton adds a finer-grained version of the same test. Look for operations you do several times a minute that carry high friction, and reduce their cost; weigh not just keystrokes but cognitive cost, meaning how many decisions and UI concepts an operation makes you think about and when. Playscii's spacebar popup for picking a character and colour, which can be docked as persistent UI, came out of that audit ([JP LeBreton 2019, 8:55](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=535)).

### Techniques for a fast loop

- **Share data between editor and game.** In Playscii a game object refers to the very same art data object the editor works on, so a change appears in the running game instantly, without saving. LeBreton demonstrates by enlarging an animated owl's eyes in art mode and flipping straight back to game mode; character sets and palettes hot-reload too ([JP LeBreton 2019, 12:29](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=749)). Playscii also exposes a Python REPL console and lets game code modify art at runtime, so you can run a cellular automaton directly on an art document, step by step or over simulated time ([JP LeBreton 2019, 14:39](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=879)).
- **Make editing and playing one keystroke apart.** One of the first things Liotta built for his roguelike puzzle in the 2017 MIT Mystery Hunt was a level editor that jumped instantly between editing a level and playing it, which let him try many quick ideas and judge each one ([Colin Liotta 2018, 8:44](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=524)).
- **Balance the live game.** Chris McCormick attaches a handler to every on-screen item and monster in Smallest Quest that dumps the object to the browser's developer console. From there he edits it live: a food item goes from 5 to 10 food before he picks it up, and a bat's damage goes to 20 and kills him in one hit. The point is balancing without restarting ([Chris McCormick 2021, 24:15](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1455)).

### A dashboard derived from the data

Spry Fox's design dashboard, described by Kemp, is the most developed example of making the game's data visible. It is an HTML page that reads the generated configs and offers sortable, filterable views of them. The item view lists all of roughly 8,800 generated items with search and toggleable property columns, and each item carries a button that opens, in VS Code, the source config that produced it; the dashboard has become the team's first stop when investigating an issue ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 16:54](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1014)). Because loot tables are authored by tag (authors describe the kinds of item to drop, not specific items), the dashboard can resolve what could actually drop and show a "dropped by" column listing every table that can produce a given item, which traces an unexpected item back to its source ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 18:14](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1094)). For their real-time calendar games, a timeline view draws the scheduled scenarios from a calendar YAML file, colour-coded with durations, so designers can see whether every day has enough for the player to do ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 20:59](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1259)).

The deeper argument is about where truth lives. Cozy Grove's hand-maintained progression spreadsheet was hugely useful but a lot of work, and it drifted out of sync with the game. With a dashboard generated from the configs there is one source of truth, the game data, and the views update themselves; local copies serve designers mid-iteration and a hosted copy serves non-designers and QA ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 26:14](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=1574)). Spreadsheets still have a place as analysis tools. Pagnutti's advice for colour-scaling a stat table is a small example of making a view honest: apply conditional formatting per stat, since speed and skill are not compared directly, and leave ranges whose values are all identical uncoloured so they do not wash out the information ([Johnathon Pagnutti 2026, 6:20](https://youtu.be/DbZe8rWviS0?t=380)).

### Tooling for procedural generators

A generator is a tool in its own right, and the talks that discuss building one for others agree on two things: build it from small parts, and accept that making it pleasant to use is real work.

Egart argues that procgen tools should be made of modular, self-contained, reusable steps with exposed parameters, like Lego pieces: the more interconnectable the pieces, the more expressive the tool. His binary space partitioning (BSP) node, for example, exposes the minimum and maximum region size ([Spencer Egart 2021, 9:23](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=563)). He built his dungeon generator as a visual node graph in Unity using the open-source xNode framework, getting drag-and-drop working in a couple of hours. The graph runs left to right from a blank level through BSP, prefab rooms and A* hallways to a node that places the player spawn, showing that steps that are not geometry belong in the same pipeline ([Spencer Egart 2021, 5:14](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=314)). His warning is that the secretly hard part is making such a tool friendly to work with, so lean on frameworks that handle the UI; he points to Dungeon Architect, xNode and a similar procedural engine for Unity ([Spencer Egart 2021, 10:02](https://youtu.be/YfLYPIXGF7E?t=602)). Pepers names the people who do this work "artificers": like a D&D artificer making a wand a peasant can use, they wrap generation in sliders, buttons and labels so others can use it without rethinking what content is, and she calls it a distinct and valuable skill ([Alexei Pepers 2019, 11:32](https://youtu.be/mYMdMAvTHpo?t=692)).

Hidden Door applies the same decomposition to a large language model. Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster describe resolving a player's stated intent through many small composable tasks instead of one LLM call: the LLM suggests outcomes, offers ideas and renders prose, while ordered tools built from classic machine learning, procgen and handwritten rules decide whether dice are needed (not to open a cabinet), adjust mood, drama, pacing and genre, and check world physics and plot needs ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 19:50](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1190)). The payoff is interpretability. Because each component is small, each can be inspected and tuned independently, like a series of lenses, which compensates for how poorly an LLM explains itself; the team also built a shared vocabulary of story coherence, agency, replayability and pacing so several disciplines could tune different parts toward one goal ([Brianna McHorse and Chris Foster 2023, 28:05](https://youtu.be/aJC3ioashbs?t=1685)).

Smaller examples show the same instinct to open the generator up:

- Sonat Uzun is building a tool that shows the parts and motifs behind each song in Tea Garden and can force the generator to use particular motifs, for fine-tuning ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 25:24](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1524)).
- Emily Halina's work-in-progress Godot tool for Tree-based Reconstructive Partitioning (TRP) runs Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) from a list of inputs and a default reward function to generate level variants during development; she admits a small example yields similar-looking levels, but says it is enough for ideation ([Emily Halina 2024, 27:27](https://youtu.be/KWBpQz1mHcA?t=1647)).
- Martin Austwick is building a pipeline that exports Twine stories as JSON into Python to render branching, procedurally generated narratives as podcast audio for Neutrinowatch ([Jeff Emtman and Martin Austwick 2024, 31:18](https://youtu.be/1sZlIfCcz_c?t=1878)).

### Building tools, and sharing them

LeBreton's design rule for Playscii is worth borrowing: rather than limit an editor to what old hardware could do, build a more powerful one and write a little code to export down to the simpler format when authenticity matters. He wanted layers, alpha blending, a CRT filter and a built-in engine with off-grid objects, which REXPaint, PabloDraw and PETSCII editors did not offer ([JP LeBreton 2019, 7:21](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=441)). In the same spirit Playscii's native format is JSON so other engines can parse it, with plugins for PNG and legacy ANSI formats ([JP LeBreton 2019, 22:43](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=1363)). REXPaint itself shows what a shared tool can do for the genre: Josh Ge built it because nothing had the features he needed, other developers use it for UI mock-ups and mapping, and he uses it every day in every aspect of Cogmind ([Josh Ge 2016, 11:00](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=660)).

The caution comes from Nifflas. His expression-driven music tool works for him, but most of the work is writing undocumented expressions that only someone who knows the software inside out could write, so releasing it would need documentation, UX work, funding and a collaborator ([Nifflas 2025, 29:19](https://youtu.be/WbgdXalXPus?t=1759)). An internal tool's speed for its author is not usability for anyone else.

## Catching problems before players do: validation and automated play

Once content lives in data, so do its mistakes, often in how independently authored pieces fit together ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 20:19](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1219)). The answer the talks give is to check automatically, at two levels: the data, statically, before it is checked in; and the game, by having a machine play it.

### Validate data where independent pieces meet

Jurie Horneman's case is a tag-based level system in which levels request rooms by tag. To guarantee a level never asks for a room that does not exist, he rejected optional tags, grey-box placeholder rooms and manual testing after every change, and instead wrote a Python script that loads the level data and the room list and reports every request without a match. Hooked into continuous integration (Jenkins, say), it means bad data is never checked in ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 5:29](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=329)). He generalises the lesson: static validation is always useful, but it matters most where independently authored assets, often from different disciplines, only meet inside the system (levels need rooms, situations need quests), and it should ideally run on every data submission ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 20:19](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1219)).

He is equally clear that it can be expensive. Static analysis is really data mining, and proving that a dynamic location-reservation system would never run out of locations on a large project turned out to be far harder than it sounded. He had to learn a system he had not written, write C++ and Python to export quest and location data, reconcile lockups QA found with his spreadsheet (false negatives), build synthetic games to confirm predicted failures (false positives), rerun the analysis whenever data changed, and still add a runtime fallback so saves would not break forever ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 8:51](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=531)). Cheap cross-reference checks pay off quickly; proofs about dynamic behaviour may not.

Several teams have built the cheap kind into their pipelines, each in a different shape:

- **Validators in the config loader.** Spry Fox's open-sourced DarkConfig library turns YAML configs into gameplay data with hot loading, validates the YAML syntax, and serves as a platform for writing game-specific validators that define what good and bad data look like ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 4:39](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=279)).
- **A schema generated from types.** Rose's Hitchhiker's Guide to the Cataclysm has to track a game with more than 300 changes a month, some of which change data shapes (numbers becoming strings with units). Hand-writing a schema for over 100 object types and 1,000 properties would be a nightmare, so a library generates a JSON schema from the guide's TypeScript types. A GitHub Action pulls each experimental release, renders every page checking for errors and validates all the game data against the schema; it has caught errors in the schema and some in the game's own data ([Jeremy Rose 2022, 16:49](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1009)).
- **Examples that are also tests and docs.** Bucklew and Frang describe how Caves of Qud attaches example input/output pairs to each text replacer as C# attributes (pass the frogs faction, expect "frogs"). The suite runs as unit tests, emits an XML reference of every replacer and its examples with errors listed first, and stops old pre-1.0 helpers from silently drifting ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:46:03](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6363)).
- **Compile the data.** NetHack's special levels go through a level compiler, chosen partly so level files would not sit readable as hints on shared multi-user systems, and partly so mistakes are caught at compile time rather than at runtime ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 23:04](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=1384)).

### Let a machine play the game

The second level of checking is to run the game itself many times. Phenry Ewing describes how Neo Cab's whole design lived in the ink narrative language, so the team could run the actual game headlessly from the command line with a JavaScript runner that made random choices, thousands of times, instead of building a separate model of it. Each run output its core variables and inputs, which they sliced into reports such as how many runs finished and how often game overs came from running out of fuel or money ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 26:56](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1616)). This is one of the payoffs of keeping the simulation separate from its presentation, described earlier in the chapter: if the game can run without a screen, you can drive it.

> Instead of building a model of the game we had one and could drive it. — [Phenry Ewing 2022, 26:56](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1616)

Kingsford goes further with an MCTS player as an automated playtester. Ask it "is this winnable?", simulating to the end of a level, a sensible turn limit or death rather than whole games, and use generic rewards such as reaching the next level and losing health, because the more closely the reward is tied to the current rules, the less it helps as the rules change. He imagines a 7DRL (a roguelike made in seven days) in which, from day one, every file save triggers the game to try for a win in the background while you watch the @ work its way through ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 21:32](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1292)). Because his game state is pure, the same agent can also fuzz: play to some point, then fire random playouts from every following turn in parallel to see whether anything throws ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 22:08](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1328)).

He is candid about the limits. The agent optimises for the reward you give it, so it plays optimally rather than like a human and cannot tell you whether the game is fun, though rewarding "fun" behaviours, such as grabbing a novelty weapon, can make it more human-like. Its value is making sure human playtesters, whose time is precious, never waste it on a broken build ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 22:27](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1347)). And MCTS needs very fast simulation loops: the logic may have to be in a compiled language rather than Python, Lua or Ruby, and multi-threaded. Kingsford learned Rust for roughly a tenfold speedup that paid off when renting AWS compute; multi-threading one tree brings locking problems he flags without solving ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 15:20](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=920)).

Oliver Withington's advice for generators belongs here too: make them easy to test by keeping them modular and able to output content in the minimal encoded form needed to evaluate it, without set dressing. Future you, he says, will be very happy ([Oliver Withington 2024, 15:12](https://youtu.be/Ls9wksddN5c?t=912)).

### When verification is out of reach

Reed's account of The Hobbit is the counterexample. Its emergent character simulation was so hard to inspect that debugging meant squinting at memory dumps, and the testers trying to verify it was bug-free or winnable gave up. It shipped with infamous bugs: Elrond's weight was unset so Bilbo could carry him, Bard could refuse to slay the dragon, Thorin behaved like a kleptomaniac. Reed notes that this also lent the game its charm ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 20:54](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=1254)). NetHack shows the defensive alternative when you cannot enumerate every state: its code handles cases its developers believe cannot happen, such as two-weaponing a corpse, and Pepers credits that with the game's rarity of crashes under bizarre player behaviour ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 17:05](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1025)).

### In practice: what to automate first

1. Cross-reference checks between independently authored data (every tag request has a matching asset), run in CI on every submission ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 5:29](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=329); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 20:19](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1219)).
2. Schema or validator checks in the loader, generated from your types where you can ([Patrick Kemp 2023, 4:39](https://youtu.be/rWPJ5fW1UH8?t=279); [Jeremy Rose 2022, 16:49](https://youtu.be/ziN33iMQVPo?t=1009)).
3. Examples attached to small text or rule helpers, run as tests ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:46:03](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=6363)).
4. Headless random or search-driven playthroughs of the real game, once the simulation can run without its presentation, aimed at crashes and winnability rather than fun ([Phenry Ewing 2022, 26:56](https://youtu.be/Nnx33ctSmRA?t=1616); [Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 21:32](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1292); [Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 22:27](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=1347)).
5. Proofs about dynamic runtime behaviour only when the stakes justify the cost, and with a runtime fallback anyway ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 8:51](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=531)).

## Seeing inside a running game: debugging, logging and telemetry

A hand-built level can be opened in an editor and looked at. A procedural game has no such scene: the thing that went wrong existed once, for one seed, in one player's run. Visibility has to be built in. Alexander Birke makes the case from Sea of Rifts: a systemic procedural game needs an easily extensible debug menu and visualisations early. Sea of Rifts has a tree-structured debug menu, reuses the in-game map to visualise generation, and has a text debug console into which a component can inject commands to rerun the same conditions; because it takes text, team members have built their own debug menus on an Elgato Stream Deck from text macros ([Alexander Birke 2024, 8:38](https://youtu.be/0jFzBf0mCRY?t=518)).

### Record everything, analyse later

Per-decision debug output only goes so far. Horneman points out that with dynamic content selection, each individual pick can be fine while the picks add up over time to a bad experience. You need to log the selection inputs through analytics and analyse them over time, which also lets you retroactively test alternative weights; without that data his teams could only tweak a weight and hope ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 18:46](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1126)).

Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup has the most mature version of this. Malloy describes how every online game emits machine-readable *milestones* (entering a new area, killing a unique, changing god) carrying race, god, level, top skill, killer and the killer's weapon into a database. Morgue files and replays suit humans, not programs; the milestone database, queried through the IRC bot Sequell with a Crawl-specific query language, lets anyone ask targeted questions about any subset of online games without writing SQL ([Alan Malloy 2017, 12:55](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=775)). The Blaseball archivists of SIBR, Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi, give the rule behind recording so much: keep everything as raw as possible before you start carving it down, because a remarkable player can break out in a single game and data that seems unimportant today may be the core of tomorrow's story ([Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:44](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=224)). Raw recordings also find uses nobody planned. Drew Streib reports that nethack.alt.org (NAO) holds roughly 200 GB of ttyrec terminal recordings, which have fed analytics and bots, one of which ascended on a public server ([Drew Streib 2016, 20:08](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1208)).

> Data you don't think is important today might be at the core of a story you want to tell tomorrow. — [Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi 2021, 3:44](https://youtu.be/WeRCGy3-uPY?t=224)

### Public servers as debugging infrastructure

Servers that host other people's games turn out to be the best crash reporters a roguelike can have. Crawl's online servers post every crash to the developer IRC channel with the morgue, stack trace and save file, and auto-update to trunk so a fixed bug does not recur for players; Malloy jokes "who needs tests when you have players", but says trunk is stable, and crashes that arrive with everything needed to reproduce them are far easier to fix than ones you have to coax out of offline players ([Alan Malloy 2017, 23:07](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=1387)). Streib makes the same point about NAO: with thousands of games a month, a one-in-a-thousand bug shows up on the server even if no individual player ever hits it, which has made NAO a useful feed of core dumps for the NetHack DevTeam ([Drew Streib 2016, 16:02](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=962)).

If you run such a server, Streib's experience covers the plumbing:

- **dgamelaunch** is a generic front end for any TTY game. It forks a ttyrec spooling process alongside each game so others can watch, and its only player interaction is simple in-game mail; the website and IRC bots run outside the jail ([Drew Streib 2016, 13:11](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=791)).
- **Security** is a headache. Game binaries have bugs, options editors must be locked down so they cannot write arbitrary files, and the game server should be kept apart from other services because it has "enough holes to drive trucks through". Back up often and get a co-admin ([Drew Streib 2016, 15:26](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=926)).
- **Hosting**: NAO stays on simple Linux instances rather than containers or serverless, because live watching needs fast open sockets and Streib avoids patching the stock game binaries; moving to AWS got him out of the hardware-failure business ([Drew Streib 2016, 17:00](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1020)).

### Legible code is a debugging tool

The cheapest visibility is code that explains itself. Pepers found NetHack's source shockingly well commented: files such as display.c open with paragraphs in plain English describing exactly what the code does, and inline comments run through whole functions such as sacrifice handling, so a developer can learn the design without knowing C ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 9:01](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=541)). Its comments also use ASCII grid diagrams for spatial behaviour: the boomerang's flight path (reverse the rows for clockwise), polearm range as a numbered grid, and how a ball and chain should move. Pepers suggests any grid-based game can steal the technique ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 15:51](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=951)).

At the far end of the scale, bhauth argues that DCSS has had development effort comparable to a AAA game, spent on what hardcore players and programmers value: online and offline play, statistics, logs, leaderboards, spectating, Lua scripting, macros and search ([bhauth 2020, 16:00](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=960)). Much of that list is the same recording and visibility infrastructure that serves its developers.

## Choosing a foundation: languages, engines and libraries

The talks spend surprisingly little time on which language or engine to use, and what they do say mostly lowers the stakes.

### Your values, or your platforms

At one end, JP LeBreton argues that building your own engine or tool is valuable less for autonomy than for putting your own values into practice. He calls the big engines tools for converting money into content, designed around business models, and argues for a flourishing of small tools with distinct identities, focus or approachability, like those found on itch.io ([JP LeBreton 2019, 17:48](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=1068)). One value he built into Playscii's engine: impose as few speed-related restrictions on behaviour as possible and make the remaining ones easy to lift, because designers exploit whatever is cheap. In Doom, moving floors and ceilings was basically free, so level designers used it everywhere, for elevators, collapsing floors and rising staircases ([JP LeBreton 2019, 13:33](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=813)).

At the other end, Biskup chose Unity for Ultimate ADOM because the team judged it the best platform for a multi-platform plan (a detailed desktop game, mobile-first iOS and Android versions, consoles later) after finding their own hand-written ports of ADOM very hard and buggy ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 13:38](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=818)). The choice depends on what you need most: control over how your tool thinks, or reach across platforms you cannot afford to port to by hand.

### Starting out

Josh Ge's advice to beginners is that the language matters little: roguelikes have been made in nearly every language, so use one you know, and if starting fresh, Python is the easiest recommendation; C and C++ have resources, but he does not recommend them to beginners who want to make a game rather than debug ([Josh Ge 2018, 2:17](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=137)). With Python, libtcod supplies both general game-library features and roguelike heavy lifting (map generation, field of view, pathfinding), each replaceable later. Ultima Ratio Regum and Temple of Torment both began from the libtcod tutorial's game, and Armoured Commander's developer went from limited programming experience to a finished, press-covered game in a year ([Josh Ge 2018, 13:36](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=816)).

Phillip Daigle, learning to program for Rogue's Gate, came to a different choice. He rejected Python as slow to show visible results beyond ASCII, C, Go and Java as a high barrier, and Unity and Unreal as heavy and too hand-holding, and found a sweet spot in GameMaker Studio 2, which handles assets, memory and sprites while still requiring real programming. His caveats: it costs money, older documentation may not match the version, at the time it lacked structs and try/catch and could not use libtcod or pygame, and he would probably pick Godot if starting over ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 9:36](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=576)).

McCormick makes the case for the browser. It is everywhere, needs no compile step, supports live reloading, and comes with images, SVG, WebGL, fonts, touch and mouse input, CSS animation and a developer console for modifying data structures in real time, which makes code portable and players easy to reach ([Chris McCormick 2021, 6:35](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=395)). With rot.js (the Roguelike Toolkit in JavaScript, by Ondřej Žára), a single script tag gives you console rendering, RNG, pathfinding, field of view, map generation, input, tile maps and scheduling; McCormick pastes the roughly 100-line tutorial result into an index.html and swaps in a tile map in about 29 more lines ([Chris McCormick 2021, 8:09](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=489)). For Java, Eben Howard presents SquidLib, an Apache 2.0 library with grid math, many dungeon generators and coloured glyph display, in a modular libGDX-based 3.0 line that also targets the web and an older Swing-based line ([Various 2018, 20:28](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1228)). And if what you want to make is a generative Twitter bot, Joe Sondow notes it needs no code at all with Cheap Bots Done Quick, built on Compton's Tracery grammar, or can be hosted free on AWS Lambda with DynamoDB for state, though many AWS "free" services expire after a year ([Joe Sondow 2017, 11:34](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=694)).

### Perspective

The tools have always shaped what was possible. Ken Arnold wrote the curses library as one abstraction over cursor-addressable terminals, building on the terminal database Bill Joy wrote for vi, so programs did not need rewriting per terminal; Rogue could not have existed without it ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 5:47](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=347)). Biskup describes writing early ADOM by "neolithic programming": no syntax highlighting, auto-completion, refactoring tools, easy version control or internet help, typing code for hours or days before a minutes-long compile returned hundreds of errors at once ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 3:03](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=183)). Any modern choice is a long way from that.

### In practice

- If you already know a language, use it ([Josh Ge 2018, 2:17](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=137)).
- If you are starting fresh and want ASCII quickly, Python with libtcod ([Josh Ge 2018, 13:36](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=816)); in the browser, JavaScript with rot.js ([Chris McCormick 2021, 8:09](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=489)); in Java, SquidLib ([Various 2018, 20:28](https://youtu.be/60MTG-__dt4?t=1228)).
- If you want sprites and an engine that does some work for you while you learn, a 2D engine such as GameMaker or Godot ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 9:36](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=576)).
- If you must ship on many platforms, weigh a large engine against the cost of hand-porting ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 13:38](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=818)).
- If you build your own, decide which values it embodies, and keep its speed restrictions few and liftable ([JP LeBreton 2019, 17:48](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=1068); [JP LeBreton 2019, 13:33](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=813)).

## Performance and hard constraints

The section on modelling entities noted that cache-friendly layouts matter little to a typical turn-based tile roguelike: when Nystrom polled his audience, only about three people had performance problems traced to cache misses ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 7:54](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=474)), and Desktop Dungeons' largest event queue is around 50 events ([Danny Day 2018, 20:18](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1218)). The talks below locate the places where performance does bite: where every entity interacts with every other, where the world is a simulated grid of cells, where a 3D scene meets a frame budget, and where the platform itself is tiny. Those edges are worth knowing, and the tightest constraints have taught techniques worth keeping.

### Where performance actually bites

**Quadratic interaction.** Knipscher found that Bioloom, an ecosystem sim, struggled at about 50 creatures because interactions such as perceiving one another scale quadratically, while the dream was a thousand. An octree did not get her past similar problems; switching to Unity DOTS had a big learning curve but gave her headroom to develop gameplay and optimise later. She notes that Burst and Jobs can be used without the full ECS ([Liza Knipscher 2025, 17:18](https://youtu.be/jBhcHdV5HHo?t=1038)).

**Cellular automata.** Anderson says that making a cellular automaton fast on modern hardware is mostly about memory, not arithmetic: keep cells small and use cache-friendly layouts such as Morton (Z-order) curves, which linearise the grid while keeping neighbours close in memory ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:33:23](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16403)). Block cellular automata are embarrassingly parallel because blocks share no data within one update, so they can run across threads (Noita uses a checkerboard of blocks) or one block per GPU thread, and dirty chunks let you skip regions that cannot change next tick, such as all-empty or all-solid ones ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:34:25](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16465)). Ian Holmes's Nematode shows how far the approach can be pushed: its whole persistent, multiplayer world, with gases, polymers and rigid bodies, runs inside a cellular automaton, with multiplayer built on the TeaTime model from Croquet in JavaScript with a Node back end ([Ian Holmes 2017, 11:13](https://youtu.be/b2VkgcC1xRc?t=673)).

**Many objects.** Biskup reports that Ultimate ADOM's Java prototype with a couple of million objects ran about a hundred times faster than the C# version; he does not know why and puts it down to the team's inexperience with C# performance. He worries more about engine complexity in Unity than about graphics, because separating the engine from its graphical interpretation is something they have already learned ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 34:23](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=2063)).

**Bounding the work.** Two talks reduce the problem rather than speed up the code. Todd Furmanski's Forska is a first-person point-and-click game: a click raycasts to a point and renders a static image from a real-time scene graph, so the game has fractions of a second per click for simulation and AI instead of a sixtieth of a second per frame, which he found liberating ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 9:21](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=561)). LeBreton added rooms to Playscii to organise a larger world and limit the scope of simulation and rendering ([JP LeBreton 2019, 16:00](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=960)).

### Field of view: efficiency against correctness

Field of view (FOV) is the classic roguelike algorithm where cost and correctness trade against each other, and Albert Ford's comparison makes the trade visible. Raycasting, casting a ray in every direction and stopping at obstacles, is essentially repeated line of sight, so it agrees with targeting, but it oversamples tiles near the viewer, as a heat map shows ([Albert Ford 2020, 2:14](https://youtu.be/y1zkrTcNJbc?t=134)). Shadowcasting scans outward in concentric squares by quadrant or octant and visits each visible tile about once (only the seams between quadrants twice), but by default it is inconsistent with line of sight at wall corners, so something can shoot you that you cannot see ([Albert Ford 2020, 3:21](https://youtu.be/y1zkrTcNJbc?t=201)). Ford's fix has two parts. Treat walls as beveled diamonds, cutting off the corners that caused the inconsistent occlusion; and reveal a tile only when its centre is visible, rather than any part of it, which makes the result symmetric. The outcome is an FOV that is efficient, consistent and symmetric ([Albert Ford 2020, 5:20](https://youtu.be/y1zkrTcNJbc?t=320)).

> What you want is to only reveal tiles where you can see the center. — [Albert Ford 2020, 5:20](https://youtu.be/y1zkrTcNJbc?t=320)

### 3D asset budgets

Roguelikes built in 3D from bought or modular assets face a different budget. Sergio Garces, building procedural 3D environments on a budget, gives a checklist:

- **Textures** are the main memory cost. Shrink them, since the difference is often invisible at play distance, and pack ambient occlusion, roughness and metallic maps into the RGB channels of one texture; colour and normal maps cannot be packed ([Sergio Garces 2022, 9:50](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=590)).
- **Geometry**: add level-of-detail (LOD) meshes to purchased assets that lack them and trim excess triangles even at the highest LOD; use shader-complexity and texture-density debug views to find expensive or oversized assets ([Sergio Garces 2022, 10:59](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=659)).
- **Draw calls** are the main 3D performance problem. Scatter small repeated objects (grass, bricks, distant buildings) as foliage with varied position, rotation and size and render them as instanced meshes, so a thousand copies cost one draw call ([Sergio Garces 2022, 16:29](https://youtu.be/6U8c6hbVJLY?t=989)).

Birke reports the same draw-call problem from kit-based ships in Sea of Rifts, and the same family of fix: combine meshes per ship family, which works because each family shares a few texture atlases ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 21:12](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1272)).

### Constraints as craft

Older and smaller platforms forced techniques that remain useful. Greg L's starting point is that numbers on a computer are rows of on/off switches with operations on them, not mathematical numbers; understanding that unlocks effects on constrained platforms ([Greg L 2026, 3:13](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=193)). Concretely:

- **Bitfields.** Pack many yes/no flags into one integer and test them with a bitwise AND. His example is a PICO-8 minimap that ANDs a "visited" value with a single-bit mask to decide whether to draw a room; the same pattern appears in controller input and collision layers ([Greg L 2026, 7:22](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=442)).
- **Wraparound.** Fixed-width integers wrap, which is why 8-bit games like The Legend of Zelda cap values at 255 and why adding one to 127 in a signed byte yields -128 ([Greg L 2026, 10:56](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=656)).
- **Fixed point.** PICO-8 uses 16.16 fixed point, in which the low bits represent halves, quarters and eighths; it behaves like integer math with an adjustment after multiplication ([Greg L 2026, 15:02](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=902)).
- **Bit tricks on floats.** The Quake III fast inverse square root reads a float's bits as an integer, shifts right to halve the exponent and subtracts from a magic constant to negate it and correct the bias, landing within about 3% before any refinement ([Greg L 2026, 26:56](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=1616)).

Greg argues these tricks are becoming more relevant, not less, because modern graphics hardware relies on them, down to Nvidia's four-bit floating-point format ([Greg L 2026, 29:08](https://youtu.be/oj3xA28N60I?t=1748)).

The genre's history is full of fitting into too little memory. Dan Stormont and Michael Howk found that the earliest Hack ran its level generator as a separate binary because the whole game would not fit into PDP-11 memory; a later refactored iteration ran as one ([Dan Stormont and Michael Howk 2026, 7:08:17](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=25697)). Keni wrote an automatic overlay system for NetHack's Amiga port using a modified GCC, replacing the PC port's intrusive per-function overlay declarations that broke often, but never released it because licensing would have meant shipping all of GCC with a game that was already the largest thing on comp.sources.games ([Jesse Collet et al. 2023, 26:23](https://youtu.be/9V_CkJ66uJQ?t=1583)). Jeff Olson built Alphaman in QuickBasic on an IBM XT to fit on one floppy and run without a maths coprocessor, so he replaced sines and cosines with integer multiplication and bit shifts and added QuickC modules with embedded assembly when the executables outgrew a 5.25-inch disk ([Jeff Olson 2023, 17:16](https://youtu.be/Gk5uWXBANkA?t=1036)).

Modern fantasy platforms impose constraints on purpose, and two speakers find them productive. PICO-8's 8,192-token limit pushed Sonat Uzun to keep Tea Garden's music generator to about 1,500 tokens through heavy code sharing: all motifs go through the same iterative loop and all parts use the same write function, and he says the limit helped him invent motif-based generation ([Sonat Uzun 2022, 24:37](https://youtu.be/SBjsVcffOHg?t=1477)). Eiríkr Åsheim describes Uxn, a small self-contained platform of assembly language, VM specification, emulators and ROMs, with 64KB of memory, 8- and 16-bit integers and a four-colour display, and finds its limitations freeing ([Eiríkr Åsheim 2024, 3:11](https://youtu.be/qogCwa12jEg?t=191)).

## Tensions and open questions

**Does ECS fit a roguelike?** Nystrom argues that domain-split ECS solves problems a turn-based tile roguelike does not have, and that almost nobody in his audience had cache-miss trouble ([Bob Nystrom 2018, 7:54](https://youtu.be/JxI3Eu5DPwE?t=474)). Biskup reports better modularisation and easier modding from a modified ECS in Ultimate ADOM ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 1:50](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=110)). They are arguing about different things: Nystrom rejects the split by engine domain and the performance case, Biskup values composition. The choice turns on whether things in your game must change what they are at runtime, such as a possessed body becoming an item or a wall coming alive, which is where components earn their cost and their class of emergent bugs ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 21:23](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1283); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 13:57](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=837); [Thomas Biskup 2018, 35:58](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=2158)). Peglin adds a caution from the other side: a component architecture that makes the team fast is not automatically a mod system ([Dylan Gedig 2022, 28:19](https://youtu.be/ke0cLTVg2_M?t=1699)).

**Coroutines or not.** Berman wants rule resolution written as coroutines so the code's call stack mirrors the game's ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 21:05](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=1265)); Cronin watched Monster Train's whole game loop become one giant coroutine tangling UI, sound and logic ([Brian Cronin 2021, 6:39](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=399)). The difference seems to be whether presentation timing goes inside the coroutine, but no talk tests a disciplined coroutine rules engine at scale.

**How far data can go.** Content as data is the chapter's strongest consensus, yet Cronin's card scripts broke down on dependent and scaling effects ([Brian Cronin 2021, 12:05](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=725)), Biskup deliberately keeps a fixed layer of core rules out of data ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 2:22](https://youtu.be/fGLJC5UY2o4?t=142)), and Ray finds that as Caves of Qud's XML grows more expressive it becomes a programming language, with a tension between power and comprehensibility that is still open ([Ray 2023, 9:46](https://youtu.be/n6mKigS_71Y?t=586)). Compton's principles for polite languages (unfoldable syntax, scaffolding, structure editors) are the best available guidance for easing that tension ([Kate Compton 2020, 20:49](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1249); [Kate Compton 2020, 21:45](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1305)), but no talk reports applying them to a large game's mod data.

**When to build structure.** Compton's rule is to introduce structure when you see the same special case written over and over, and she admits to over-engineering a parser she later abandoned ([Kate Compton 2016, 13:03](https://youtu.be/isB82kORimk?t=783); [Kate Compton 2020, 25:57](https://youtu.be/E5-3Ui7oO8U?t=1557)); Hinenzon's chore queue drifted until it did little of what it was built for ([Stav Hinenzon 2023, 11:08](https://youtu.be/MyVigc1nDig?t=668)). Against that, Moromisato, Cronin and Day all say that some things are much harder to retrofit than to design in from the start: modding hooks and API versions, determinism for previews, gameplay replays ([George Moromisato 2022, 18:48](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1128); [George Moromisato 2022, 25:49](https://youtu.be/mES03vaZo3U?t=1549); [Brian Cronin 2021, 8:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=486); [Danny Day 2018, 22:21](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1341)). The talks suggest the line falls between speculative generality, which you should defer, and the few properties (determinism, serialisable state, a versioned extension point) that are cheap early and very expensive late.

**Retrofitting an existing codebase.** No talk offers a clean path from a coupled codebase to an isolated simulation. Biskup concluded ADOM could not be separated and built a new engine ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 9:24](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=564)); Russ spent about a year making NetHack's saves forward-compatible ([Tariq et al. 2016, 12:22](https://youtu.be/SDojcmObQzw?t=742)); Day found replays too complicated to add late ([Danny Day 2018, 22:21](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=1341)). Incremental steps exist, such as giving UI handlers the lowest priority ([Danny Day 2018, 13:22](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=802)) and categorised logging while you live with the coupling ([Brian Cronin 2021, 25:41](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=1541)), but how to get from there to a black-box simulation remains unsolved.

**Rollback or lockstep.** Zeyfang needed rollback because NecroDancer's rhythm cannot wait a round trip ([Adrian Zeyfang 2024, 3:03](https://youtu.be/zwhNSbFVKQM?t=183)); Plummer lost two months to rollback before lockstep proved enough for a turn-based game ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 8:47](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=527)). The deciding factor is how much input latency the game can tolerate.

**Animation order.** Reid calls synchronising animations with the logical order of simultaneous events the hardest part of juicing a roguelike and left the glitches in Golden Krone Hotel ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 27:58](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1678)). Thomas Robertson's blocking and concurrent effect lists are a plausible general answer ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 5:10](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=310)), but no talk shows a full scheduler that derives ordering from the simulation's change records.

**Own engine or big engine.** LeBreton argues for building your own engine or tool to put your values into practice ([JP LeBreton 2019, 17:48](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=1068)); Biskup chose Unity for multi-platform reach after painful hand-written ports ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 13:38](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=818)). It depends on whether control over how your tool thinks or reach across platforms matters more.

**Which language.** Josh Ge says language matters little and recommends Python with libtcod to beginners ([Josh Ge 2018, 2:17](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=137); [Josh Ge 2018, 13:36](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=816)); Daigle rejected Python as slow to show visible results beyond ASCII and chose GameMaker, though he would pick Godot now ([Phillip Daigle 2020, 9:36](https://youtu.be/2C3w7-SU5ek?t=576)). And Kingsford's tree-search playtesting needed a compiled, multi-threaded loop, with the locking problems of a shared search tree left unsolved ([Lachlan Kingsford 2026, 15:20](https://youtu.be/9iTJ9Z8p0ao?t=920)). Language matters little for writing the game and can matter a lot for the tools that play it thousands of times.

**Little languages and their learning cost.** Kovach frames a restrictive language as a conduct that forces new and useful ways of thinking ([Scott Kovach 2019, 13:18](https://youtu.be/s9Wyn9BJJI4?t=798)); Cooper's small user study gave some indication that identity-free tile rewriting asks for a different way of thinking about program structure than a player object does ([Seth Cooper 2025, 15:54](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=954)). Whether the bill is worth paying depends on how closely the language's constraints match the problem.

**How much to verify.** Cross-reference validation is cheap and catches real errors ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 5:29](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=329); [Jurie Horneman 2023, 20:19](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=1219)), but Horneman's attempt to prove a dynamic reservation system never ran dry cost far more than expected and still needed a runtime fallback ([Jurie Horneman 2023, 8:51](https://youtu.be/FV_0rmqxbxw?t=531)). At the far end, The Hobbit's simulation could not be verified at all, shipped with famous bugs that Reed says also lent it charm ([Aaron A. Reed 2023, 20:54](https://youtu.be/CE7o3GGif30?t=1254)), while NetHack handles cases its developers believe impossible and rarely crashes ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 17:05](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1025)). How much emergent misbehaviour a game can afford is a design decision as much as an engineering one.

**Tooling still missing.** Caves of Qud's translators work in raw XML with no in-game view of a string in context, and the team calls such tooling a big unknown ([Brian Bucklew and Corey Frang 2026, 1:59:54](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=7194)). Anderson's sparse "hash sand" storage for falling-sand worlds is an untested idea ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:37:44](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16664)).

## Checklist

- Where is the giant chain of if statements in your content code, and what data structure would replace it?
- Can a designer add an item, monster or card by editing data alone, and what does it cost when they cannot?
- Are timing values and other tuning that shapes the player's experience in data, or buried in code where only programmers can reach them?
- Does adding a new behaviour require touching existing ones, or can it be added as a new action, command or handler?
- If your events have an order, is it deterministic and documented, and can you replay an event log to see what happened?
- Does any simulation code call into UI, animation or sound, and does the presentation ever write back into game state?
- Is all simulation state, including the random number generator, in one structure you can serialise, copy and compare?
- Can you reproduce a player's bug from their save or replay, and run the game headlessly for automated play?
- Does your networking model match your game's real tolerance for input lag?
- If you want mods, is your own content built with the mod system, and does every mod declare an API version?
- What is the turnaround for your most frequent edit, and which operation do you do several times a minute that could be cheaper?
- Does any hand-maintained spreadsheet duplicate data the game already has?
- Is cross-referenced data (tags, IDs, room requests) validated in continuous integration on every submission?
- Do you have an extensible debug menu, and do you record the inputs to dynamic content selection so you can analyse them later?
- Do crashes from players arrive with a save and a stack trace attached?
